- **Chunk = 1024 bytes; block = 64 bytes** [spec]: "The input of BLAKE3 is split into contiguous chunks of 1024 bytes… Each chunk of up to 1024 bytes is split into blocks of up to 64 bytes." — BLAKE3 paper §2.1/§2.4, https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3-specs/blob/master/blake3.pdf; mirrored in the C2SP spec https://github.com/C2SP/C2SP/blob/main/BLAKE3.md

- **Explicit rationale exists** — paper §7.1 "Chunk Size" [spec]:

The chunk size is a tradeoff between the peak throughput for long inputs, which benefits from larger chunks, and the degree of parallelism for medium-length inputs, which benefits from shorter chunks. The benefit of a larger chunk size is that the tree contains fewer parent nodes, so the overhead cost of compressing them is lower… The benefit of a smaller chunk size is a higher potential degree of parallelism… Consider an 8 KiB input. With a chunk size of 1 KiB, this input can occupy 8 SIMD lanes, which lets the implementation use AVX2… But if we increased the chunk size to 2 KiB, the same input would only occupy 4 SIMD lanes… Thus we want to pick the smallest chunk size we can to maximize medium-length parallelism, without incurring 'excessive' overhead from parent nodes… **In our measurements, we find that implementations with 1 KiB chunks can reach at least 90% of that peak throughput** [vs. a 64 KiB chunk size where parent-node overhead is negligible]."

**No rigorous published measurements of chunk size vs. per-chunk overhead vs. ranged-fetch waste were found from any official IPFS source.** What exists:

1. Why exactly 256 KiB — no authoritative rationale anywhere; IPIP-499 says it was picked in the go-ipfs alpha and never contested.

Here's the full detail.

**Leaf sizing is exactly determined.** `seal_chunk` emits `nonce(24) || ciphertext || tag(16)` (`chunk.rs:65`, `aead.rs:15,17`), and ciphertext length equals plaintext length for XChaCha20-Poly1305. So:

```
sealed_leaf_len(i) = plaintext_chunk_len(i) + 40
leaf i < n-1  →  chunkSize + 40
leaf n-1      →  size - chunkSize*(n-1) + 40
empty file    →  size 0, exactly 1 leaf, 40 bytes   (chunk.rs:84-86)
n = expected_leaf_count(size, chunkSize) = ceil(size/chunkSize), or 1 when size==0   (dag.rs:207-213)
```

**The root block already carries everything needed to reconstruct that.** `decode_root` returns `{chunk_size, size, leaf_cids}` (`dag.rs:143-150`) and validates on the way through: nonzero chunk size, every link a well-formed `raw` content CID, and `links.len() == expected_leaf_count(size, chunkSize)` (`dag.rs:178-192`). So given the root block plus a concatenated leaf stream, leaf boundaries are recoverable with no additional metadata, and each parsed leaf can be checked with `compute_cid(0x55, leaf) == links[i]` — a fail-closed integrity check on the staged blob for free.

**A correction to what I said earlier, because it changes the comparison:** I called a serialized `SealedContent` "a new wire format," implying novelty was the cost. The real cost is worse and more specific. `Op` uses `serde_json` (`op.rs:181`), so serde is the established internal precedent — but `serde_json` encodes `Vec<u8>` as a JSON array of decimal numbers, roughly **4x inflation**. Harmless for a small `Op`; for multi-MB sealed content it would quadruple staged bytes and corrupt the `staged_bytes_total` budget accounting that `stage_op` gates on. So "follow the `Op` precedent" is actively the wrong move here.

Using core's det-CBOR instead avoids the inflation (CBOR byte strings are length-prefixed raw), but `encode` builds a `Value` tree (`dag.rs:116-124`) — for a multi-MB file that means materializing the whole payload as `Value::Bytes` nodes before encoding, on top of the copies `#815` is already worried about.

**One more fact that matters downstream:** `ApiClient::upload` takes one blob and returns one `UploadResult { cid, size }` (`api/client.rs:292-303`, `types.rs:197-202`). So a drain uploads **N+1 times** — every leaf, plus the root. The staged blob must therefore yield per-block byte ranges at drain regardless of which option you pick; that is not an argument between them, it's a constraint on all of them.

Storage overhead of keeping leaf CIDs explicitly, for reference: 36 bytes per leaf, so ~0.003% at a 1 MiB chunk size. Negligible either way — this decision is about robustness and memory, not size.

Fair — let me lay it out properly.

Let **S** = total sealed bytes (≈ plaintext + 40 per leaf), **n** = leaf count.

| | A: root + concat leaves | B: concat leaves only | C: det-CBOR SealedContent | D: key per block |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Peak mem, seal | ~2S | ~2S | **~3S** (leaves + Value tree + output) | **~S + chunk** (stage and drop) |
| Peak mem, drain | ~S + chunk | ~S + chunk | **~3S** (blob + Value tree + extracted) | **~chunk** |
| Boundary recovery | From own root manifest | From ambient `ContentProfile` | Explicit | N/A |
| Survives chunk-size change | Yes | **No** | Yes | Yes |
| Self-integrity check | Yes, CID per leaf | **None available** | Yes | Yes |
| Resumable upload | No | No | No | **Yes, structurally** |
| Budget accuracy | Exact | Exact | Exact | Exact |
| New code | u32 framing + parser | Solver for n | Codec mapping + versioning | Rework 2 landed fns |
| Touches landed code | No | No | No | **Yes** |

**A — root block + concatenated leaves.** The root block is already a frozen, validated, self-describing artifact, so you get boundary recovery and per-leaf CID verification without inventing anything. Downside is genuinely minor: a small outer framing that will itself want a version byte eventually.

**B — concatenated leaves only.** I want to be precise about why this is worse than it looks. `size` isn't in the blob, so you'd solve for `n` and the last-leaf length from `blob_len` and the ambient chunk size. That's algebraically doable — but if chunk size ever differs from what sealed it, the solve doesn't *fail*, it produces a plausible-but-wrong split. With no stored CIDs there's nothing to catch it, so you'd re-derive a wrong root, publish it, and the version is permanently unreadable. Silent corruption rather than a loud error. That disqualifies it for me.

**C — det-CBOR `SealedContent`.** Cleanest to read at drain and uses core's codec, consistent with the "one codec" principle in `dag.rs:10`. But `encode` takes a `Value` tree, so every leaf gets cloned into `Value::Bytes` before encoding — ~3S peak on both sides. On a 100 MiB upload that's ~300 MiB resident in a browser tab.

**D — one staging key per block.** I under-sold this initially. It's the only option that structurally solves *two* problems: peak memory drops to roughly one chunk on both sides, and it makes upload **crash-resumable** — drain calls `remove_staged_bytes` as each block lands, so a retry resumes rather than re-sending the whole file. On flaky mobile with a large file that difference is significant, and A/B/C can only get it by adding separate durable progress state or a per-block "already pinned?" round trip. Its cost is real but contained: `orphan_staging_keys`' exact-match `referenced` set (`staging.rs:88-111`) and `stage_op`'s single `upload: Option<&[u8]>` parameter (`staging.rs:47-52`) both need rework, and both are landed and tested.

**The structural point, which I think outranks the comparison:** every axis that separates these — peak memory, whether you hold the whole payload at once, whether upload is chunk-at-a-time — is *exactly* what [the memory model ticket](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/815) decides. If #815 lands on "engine frames from a full in-memory `Vec<u8>`", A is right and D is over-engineering. If it lands on streaming or a bounded-memory model, D stops being optional. Deciding the blob shape first would prejudge #815 from the wrong end.

So I don't think this should be resolved inside #814 at all.

**Kubo config** (`Import.UnixFSChunker`), verbatim [official docs / source]:

> The maximum accepted value for `size-<bytes>` and rabin `max` parameter is `2MiB - 256 bytes` (2096896 bytes). The 256-byte overhead budget is reserved for protobuf/UnixFS framing so that serialized blocks stay within the 2MiB block size limit defined by the [bitswap spec](https://specs.ipfs.tech/bitswap-protocol/#block-sizes).
> …
> **Default: `size-262144`**

https://github.com/ipfs/kubo/blob/master/docs/config.md (`### Import.UnixFSChunker`, ~line 4038)

**boxo chunker source** [source code] — https://github.com/ipfs/boxo/blob/main/chunker/parse.go

```go
// DefaultBlockSize is the chunk size that splitters produce (or aim to).
var DefaultBlockSize int64 = 1024 * 256

// BlockSizeLimit is the maximum block size defined by the bitswap spec.
// https://specs.ipfs.tech/bitswap-protocol/#block-sizes
BlockSizeLimit int = 2 * 1024 * 1024 // 2MiB
ChunkOverheadBudget int = 256
ChunkSizeLimit int = BlockSizeLimit - ChunkOverheadBudget  // 2096896
```

**Rationale for 256 KiB specifically: NOT FOUND in any authoritative source.** The code carries no justification comment. The closest thing to an official statement is IPIP-499, which effectively says it was never reasoned about [spec]:

> "The year 2015 in the name indicates that the majority of these parameters were picked a decade ago, when the initial go-ipfs alpha software was implemented, and **these defaults were never contested since then**."
> — https://specs.ipfs.tech/ipips/ipip-0499/ §3.2

The UnixFS spec frames 256 KiB purely as legacy convention, and the constraint that actually binds is the bitswap 2 MiB ceiling [spec]:

> "Safe conventions for producing new blocks: Implementations SHOULD use 256 KiB (popular legacy size) or 1 MiB (modern maximum recommended) for newly created blocks. Decoding requirement: Implementations MUST be able to decode blocks up to 2 MiB as it is effectively the maximum message size in Bitswap, which acts as ecosystem-wide common denominator… (2025Q3)"
> "If you want to maximize the interoperability of your data, make sure to keep chunk sizes no bigger than 1 MiB."
> — https://specs.ipfs.tech/unixfs/ §5.2 Block Size Considerations

So: 256 KiB is *not* derived from the block-size limit; it is 8x below it. Only the *max* chunker value is derived from it.

## 2. Maximum block size

| Limit | Value | Source | Trust |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bitswap MUST-support | **2 MiB (2097152)** | "Bitswap implementations _MUST_ support sending and receiving individual blocks of sizes less than or equal to 2MiB. Handling blocks larger than 2MiB is not recommended so as to keep compatibility…" — https://specs.ipfs.tech/bitswap-protocol/#block-sizes | spec |
| Trustless gateway client limit | **2 MiB** | "Clients _SHOULD NOT_ download unbounded amounts of data before being able to validate that data. Clients _SHOULD_ limit the maximum block size to 2MiB." + "Blocks larger than 2MiB are not ecosystem-safe: tooling built to handle larger blocks will encounter compatibility issues with storage providers, pinning services, and other infrastructure that enforce this limit." — https://specs.ipfs.tech/http-gateways/trustless-gateway/ §7.2.1 Block Limits; §7.2.4.2 repeats it as a memory-exhaustion defense | spec |
| Production soft limit | **1 MiB** | UnixFS spec §5.2 (above): produce ≤256 KiB or ≤1 MiB, "modern maximum recommended" | spec |
| Kubo/boxo enforced chunker max | **2096896 bytes** (2 MiB − 256 B framing budget) | boxo `chunker/parse.go` `ChunkSizeLimit`; Kubo config.md | source code |
| `BlockSizeLimit` in the importer | `var BlockSizeLimit = chunker.BlockSizeLimit` → 2 MiB, commented "the bitswap spec maximum" | https://github.com/ipfs/boxo/blob/main/ipld/unixfs/importer/helpers/helpers.go | source code |

The "1 MiB soft / 2 MiB hard" framing you expected is stated most directly here [official forum, lower trust — linked *from* the trustless-gateway spec]: "Current IPFS implementations recommend users create blocks ≤1 MiB and that they are able to accept and transfer blocks ≤ 2MiB… There is no hard block limit in IPLD or specified across all IPFS implementations." — https://discuss.ipfs.tech/t/supporting-large-ipld-blocks/15093/

Note: `buzhash` has a separate fixed internal max of 512 KiB (Kubo config.md).

## 3. Fan-out — 174 links per node

boxo `ipld/unixfs/importer/helpers/helpers.go` [source code]:

```go
// rough estimates on expected sizes
var roughLinkBlockSize = 1 << 13 // 8KB
var roughLinkSize = 34 + 8 + 5   // sha256 multihash + size + no name
                                 // + protobuf framing

// DefaultLinksPerBlock governs how the importer decides how many links there
// will be per block. This calculation is based on expected distributions of:
//  - the expected distribution of block sizes
//  - the expected distribution of link sizes
//  - desired access speed
var DefaultLinksPerBlock = roughLinkBlockSize / roughLinkSize
```

Derivation: 8192 / 47 = 174.29 → **174** (Go integer division). Confirmed as the user-facing default in Kubo config.md: `Import.UnixFSFileMaxLinks` **Default: `174`**; `Import.UnixFSDirectoryMaxLinks` **Default: `174`**.

Caveat worth flagging: the comment self-labels these as "rough estimates" with no measurement or citation behind the 8 KiB target. **No authoritative rationale for why the link-block should be ~8 KiB was found.** IPIP-499 §5.2 confirms the behavioral consequence with a test vector: "File at max links: 174 × 256 KiB chunks, single-level DAG with 174 links" — i.e. a 43.5 MiB file is the largest single-level DAG.

The modern IPIP-499 `unixfs-v1-2025` profile moves to **1 MiB chunks / 1024 links**, with the only quantified rationale published anywhere official [spec]:

> "The unixfs-v1-2025 profile uses 1 MiB chunks with 1024 links per node, compared to the legacy 256 KiB chunks with 174 links. This results in: Shallower DAG trees (3 levels for a 1 TiB file vs 4 levels with legacy parameters); Approximately 4x fewer total nodes for the same content; Faster random access and seeking in large files (fewer round-trips to traverse the tree); Fewer CIDs to announce, reducing stress on public good routing infrastructure such as the Amino DHT."
> — https://specs.ipfs.tech/ipips/ipip-0499/ §4.1

This is opt-in in Kubo (`unixfs-v1-2025` profile, Kubo v0.40+); the shipped default on master is still 256 KiB / 174.

## 4. Helia / JS defaults

`@helia/unixfs` delegates to `ipfs-unixfs-importer`. Defaults [source code, https://github.com/ipfs/js-ipfs-unixfs]:

- `packages/ipfs-unixfs-importer/src/constants.ts`: `DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE_256KIB = 262_144`, `DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE_1MIB = 1_048_576`, `DEFAULT_RAW_LEAVES = true`, `DEFAULT_CID_VERSION = 1`, `DEFAULT_SHARD_FANOUT_BITS = 8`, `DEFAULT_SHARD_SPLIT_THRESHOLD_BYTES = 262_144`
- `src/chunker/fixed-size.ts`: `const chunkSize = options.chunkSize ?? DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE_256KIB` → **262144 default**
- `src/layout/balanced.ts`: `const DEFAULT_MAX_CHILDREN_PER_NODE = 174` → **174 default**
- `src/index.ts` profile switch: `'unixfs-v0-2015'` → 256 KiB / 174 / dag-pb leaves / CIDv0; `'unixfs-v1-2025'` → 1 MiB / 1024 / raw leaves / CIDv1

So JS matches Go: **256 KiB and 174 by default**, with 1 MiB/1024 available via the IPIP-499 profile. Note JS defaults `rawLeaves: true` and `cidVersion: 1` where Kubo defaults to dag-pb leaves/CIDv0 — a known cross-implementation divergence IPIP-499 exists to fix.

## 5. BLAKE3

- **Chunk = 1024 bytes; block = 64 bytes** [spec]: "The input of BLAKE3 is split into contiguous chunks of 1024 bytes… Each chunk of up to 1024 bytes is split into blocks of up to 64 bytes." — BLAKE3 paper §2.1/§2.4, https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3-specs/blob/master/blake3.pdf; mirrored in the C2SP spec https://github.com/C2SP/C2SP/blob/main/BLAKE3.md

- **Explicit rationale exists** — paper §7.1 "Chunk Size" [spec]:
  > "BLAKE3 uses 1 KiB chunks. The chunk size is a tradeoff between the peak throughput for long inputs, which benefits from larger chunks, and the degree of parallelism for medium-length inputs, which benefits from shorter chunks. The benefit of a larger chunk size is that the tree contains fewer parent nodes, so the overhead cost of compressing them is lower… The benefit of a smaller chunk size is a higher potential degree of parallelism… Consider an 8 KiB input. With a chunk size of 1 KiB, this input can occupy 8 SIMD lanes, which lets the implementation use AVX2… But if we increased the chunk size to 2 KiB, the same input would only occupy 4 SIMD lanes… Thus we want to pick the smallest chunk size we can to maximize medium-length parallelism, without incurring 'excessive' overhead from parent nodes… **In our measurements, we find that implementations with 1 KiB chunks can reach at least 90% of that peak throughput** [vs. a 64 KiB chunk size where parent-node overhead is negligible]."
  > "…verified streaming requires buffering chunks (see §6.4), and incremental updates require re-hashing chunks (see §6.5), so both of those use cases benefit from a smaller chunk size."

- **No recommended I/O granularity.** The spec prescribes no application-level read/write chunking. The only constraint on grouping is structural, from `blake3::hazmat` [official docs, https://docs.rs/blake3/latest/blake3/hazmat/]: a subtree you hash independently must be a power-of-2 multiple of `CHUNK_LEN` (1024) and start at an aligned `input_offset`. So any application chunking that wants to reuse BLAKE3 subtree CVs must use a **power-of-two multiple of 1024 bytes**, aligned — 256 KiB (2^18) and 1 MiB (2^20) both satisfy this.

## 6. Published measurements — largely absent

**No rigorous published measurements of chunk size vs. per-chunk overhead vs. ranged-fetch waste were found from any official IPFS source.** What exists:

- IPIP-499 §4.1 (above): the only official quantified claim — 3 vs 4 DAG levels for 1 TiB, ~4x fewer nodes, fewer DHT announcements. Analytic, not measured. [spec]
- Trustless gateway §7.2.1: qualitative argument *for* smaller blocks — "larger blocks increase memory pressure on resource-constrained clients and widen the window for incomplete transfers. Since blocks must be validated as a unit, smaller blocks allow for more granular verification and easier retries on failure." [spec]
- BLAKE3 §7.1: the 90%-of-peak-throughput figure (above) is the one real measurement in this whole set, though it concerns hashing overhead, not network fetch. [spec]
- **Lower trust**: https://github.com/ipfs/kubo/issues/8179 ("Increase maximum chunk size to 4mb") contains the claim "Setting the chunk size to 1mb doubles the performance over a chunk size of 256kb" — this is a *user's* enhancement request, not a maintainer statement, and carries no methodology.
- **Lower trust**: https://discuss.ipfs.tech/t/supporting-large-ipld-blocks/15093/ — official forum thread on removing block limits; states the 1 MiB/2 MiB convention but attributes it to ecosystem practice, not measurement.

1. Why exactly 256 KiB — no authoritative rationale anywhere; IPIP-499 says it was picked in the go-ipfs alpha and never contested.
2. Why the ~8 KiB link-block target that yields 174 — the boxo comment says "rough estimates" with no backing data.
3. Ranged-fetch waste as a function of chunk size — no official measurement found in specs, docs, or boxo/kubo repos.

Part of #813

## Question

`SealedContent` is a DAG root block plus N sealed leaf blocks, but the staging store holds **one opaque blob under one key** (`seams/staging_store.rs:38`) and an `Op` carries exactly **one** `content_staging_key` (`sync/op.rs:46`, `:81`). What reconciles the two?

Surfaced while resolving #814. Blocked by #815, because every axis that separates the candidates — peak memory, whether the whole payload is held at once, whether upload is chunk-at-a-time — is what the memory model decides.

## Established facts

Leaf sizing is exactly determined. `seal_chunk` emits `nonce(24) || ciphertext || tag(16)` (`content/chunk.rs:65`, `core/src/suite/aead.rs:15,17`) and ciphertext length equals plaintext length, so:

```
sealed_leaf_len(i) = plaintext_chunk_len(i) + 40
leaf i < n-1  ->  chunkSize + 40
leaf n-1      ->  size - chunkSize*(n-1) + 40
empty file    ->  size 0, exactly one leaf, 40 bytes     (chunk.rs:84-86)
n = ceil(size / chunkSize), or 1 when size == 0          (dag.rs:207-213)
```

The root block already carries what is needed to reconstruct that: `decode_root` returns `{chunk_size, size, leaf_cids}` and validates nonzero chunk size, well-formed `raw` leaf CIDs, and `links.len() == expected_leaf_count` (`dag.rs:159-199`). Leaf CIDs are derivable, not independent data — `compute_cid(CONTENT_CID_CODEC, sealed)` (`chunk.rs:94`).

A drain uploads **N+1 times**: `ApiClient::upload` takes one blob and returns one `UploadResult { cid, size }` (`api/client.rs:292-303`). Every candidate must therefore yield per-block byte ranges at drain; that is a shared constraint, not a differentiator.

Note `serde_json` — the existing internal `Op` encoding (`op.rs:181`) — is **not** a viable precedent here: it encodes `Vec<u8>` as a JSON array of decimals, roughly 4x inflation, which would quadruple staged bytes and corrupt the `staged_bytes_total` budget accounting `stage_op` gates on.

## Candidates

Let S = total sealed bytes, n = leaf count.

| | A: root + concat leaves | B: concat leaves only | C: det-CBOR SealedContent | D: key per block |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Peak mem, seal | ~2S | ~2S | ~3S | ~S + chunk |
| Peak mem, drain | ~S + chunk | ~S + chunk | ~3S | ~chunk |
| Boundary recovery | own root manifest | ambient `ContentProfile` | explicit | n/a |
| Survives chunk-size change | yes | **no** | yes | yes |
| Self-integrity check | per-leaf CID | **none** | per-leaf CID | per-leaf CID |
| Resumable upload | no | no | no | **yes** |
| New code | u32 framing + parser | solver for n | codec mapping + versioning | rework 2 landed fns |

**A — root block + concatenated leaves.** `[u32 root_len][root_block][leaf_0]...[leaf_n-1]`. Boundary recovery and per-leaf CID verification come free from an already-frozen, already-validated artifact. Wants a version byte on the outer framing eventually.

**B — concatenated leaves only.** `size` is absent from the blob, so `n` and the last-leaf length must be solved from `blob_len` and the ambient chunk size. Doable, but if chunk size ever differs from what sealed the blob the solve does not fail — it yields a plausible-but-wrong split, and with no stored CIDs nothing catches it. The result is a wrong root, published, and a permanently unreadable version. Silent corruption; recommend rejecting.

**C — det-CBOR `SealedContent`.** Cleanest at drain and consistent with the "one codec" principle (`dag.rs:10`), but `encode` takes a `Value` tree (`dag.rs:116-124`), so every leaf is cloned into `Value::Bytes` before encoding — ~3S peak on both sides.

**D — one staging key per block.** The only candidate that structurally solves both peak memory (~one chunk on both sides) and **crash-resumable upload** — drain calls `remove_staged_bytes` as each block lands, so a retry resumes instead of re-sending the file. Cost: `orphan_staging_keys`' exact-match `referenced` set (`sync/staging.rs:88-111`) and `stage_op`'s single `upload: Option<&[u8]>` parameter (`staging.rs:47-52`) both need rework, and both are landed and tested.

## How #815 decides this

If the memory model lands on "engine frames from a full in-memory `Vec<u8>`", A is right and D is over-engineering. If it lands on streaming or any bounded-memory model, D stops being optional. Resolve #815 first.

The root block already carries what is needed to reconstruct that: `decode_root` returns `{chunk_size, size, leaf_cids}` and validates nonzero chunk size, well-formed `raw` leaf CIDs, and `links.len() == expected_leaf_count` (`dag.rs:159-199`). Leaf CIDs are derivable, not independent data — `compute_cid(CONTENT_CID_CODEC, sealed)` (`chunk.rs:94`).

A drain uploads **N+1 times**: `ApiClient::upload` takes one blob and returns one `UploadResult { cid, size }` (`api/client.rs:292-303`). Every candidate must therefore yield per-block byte ranges at drain; that is a shared constraint, not a differentiator.

Note `serde_json` — the existing internal `Op` encoding (`op.rs:181`) — is **not** a viable precedent here: it encodes `Vec<u8>` as a JSON array of decimals, roughly 4x inflation, which would quadruple staged bytes and corrupt the `staged_bytes_total` budget accounting `stage_op` gates on.

## Candidates

Let S = total sealed bytes, n = leaf count.

| | A: root + concat leaves | B: concat leaves only | C: det-CBOR SealedContent | D: key per block |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Peak mem, seal | ~2S | ~2S | ~3S | ~S + chunk |
| Peak mem, drain | ~S + chunk | ~S + chunk | ~3S | ~chunk |
| Boundary recovery | own root manifest | ambient `ContentProfile` | explicit | n/a |
| Survives chunk-size change | yes | **no** | yes | yes |
| Self-integrity check | per-leaf CID | **none** | per-leaf CID | per-leaf CID |
| Resumable upload | no | no | no | **yes** |
| New code | u32 framing + parser | solver for n | codec mapping + versioning | rework 2 landed fns |

**A — root block + concatenated leaves.** `[u32 root_len][root_block][leaf_0]...[leaf_n-1]`. Boundary recovery and per-leaf CID verification come free from an already-frozen, already-validated artifact. Wants a version byte on the outer framing eventually.

**B — concatenated leaves only.** `size` is absent from the blob, so `n` and the last-leaf length must be solved from `blob_len` and the ambient chunk size. Doable, but if chunk size ever differs from what sealed the blob the solve does not fail — it yields a plausible-but-wrong split, and with no stored CIDs nothing catches it. The result is a wrong root, published, and a permanently unreadable version. Silent corruption; recommend rejecting.

**C — det-CBOR `SealedContent`.** Cleanest at drain and consistent with the "one codec" principle (`dag.rs:10`), but `encode` takes a `Value` tree (`dag.rs:116-124`), so every leaf is cloned into `Value::Bytes` before encoding — ~3S peak on both sides.

**D — one staging key per block.** The only candidate that structurally solves both peak memory (~one chunk on both sides) and **crash-resumable upload** — drain calls `remove_staged_bytes` as each block lands, so a retry resumes instead of re-sending the file. Cost: `orphan_staging_keys`' exact-match `referenced` set (`sync/staging.rs:88-111`) and `stage_op`'s single `upload: Option<&[u8]>` parameter (`staging.rs:47-52`) both need rework, and both are landed and tested.

## How #815 decides this

If the memory model lands on "engine frames from a full in-memory `Vec<u8>`", A is right and D is over-engineering. If it lands on streaming or any bounded-memory model, D stops being optional. Resolve #815 first.

## Resolution

**Candidate 1: seal at command time, stage the sealed bytes, upload at drain.**

This is ratified rather than freshly chosen — the landed code already binds it in contract text, and the ticket's three-way framing was wrong to treat it as open:

- `sync/staging.rs:40-42` — "`upload` is the **already-sealed** content payload (core's content-seal runs upstream in the content plane); no plaintext user content ever lands in the staging store at rest." Sealing therefore happens before staging, i.e. inside `Engine::command`.
- `sync/op.rs:11-13` — "Content bytes never live in an op … the bytes sit in the staging store behind the profile budget."
- The staging budget (`SyncTimingProfile::staging_budget_bytes`, enforced at `staging.rs:54-70`) exists specifically so an **offline** device can stage an upload, which only has meaning if upload is deferred past the journal.

Candidate 2 (seal and upload eagerly, journal CIDs) is excluded: it would break the offline parity `blueprint/engine.md:208-211` and `web-client.md:189-193` require — "one journaled op regardless of online state". Candidate 3 (hybrid, upload eagerly when online) collapses with it and is rejected explicitly: two code paths for one op, with no offline guarantee bought.

## Consequences to carry into the slice chain

**The over-budget error surface must be designed with the command.** `stage_and_notify` (`facade.rs:1581-1597`) currently hardcodes `upload = None` and maps `StageOutcome::RejectedOverBudget` onto an internal `EngineError::Seam`. There is no `EngineError::OverBudget` variant (`facade.rs:449-512`), so the law that "past the budget only new uploads fail fast, while metadata ops queue unbounded" (`engine.md:233-235`, restated at `staging.rs:5-9`) is currently unexpressible at the facade boundary. A content-bearing `Create`/`UpdateContent` needs a typed over-budget error carrying `{staged, incoming, budget}`, distinct from a seam failure.

**A drain uploads N+1 times.** `ApiClient::upload` takes one blob and returns one `UploadResult { cid, size }` (`api/client.rs:292-303`), so every leaf plus the root is a separate call. This is an input to the ordering-and-rollback question (#819): a partial upload is the common case, not an edge case.

## Newly surfaced

Establishing the above exposed a sharper question the ticket did not anticipate: `SealedContent` is a root block plus N leaf blocks, but the staging store holds one opaque blob under one key and an `Op` carries exactly one `content_staging_key`. Filed as #828 with the full candidate comparison, blocked by #815 — the memory model determines the answer, so deciding the blob shape first would prejudge it from the wrong end.

## Still open, deliberately

Where the per-version content key lives across the durable boundary is **not** answered here — that is #818, which this ticket unblocks. Candidate 1 is what makes it hard: the key is a KDF non-edge (`crates/core/src/kdf/mod.rs:18-20`), so it cannot be re-derived, and something must carry it from command to drain.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/myankelev/.claude/skills/wayfinder

A loose idea has arrived — too big for one agent session, and wrapped in fog: the way from here to the **destination** isn't visible yet. Wayfinding is about finding that way, not charging at the destination. This skill charts the way as a **shared map** on the repo's issue tracker, then works its **decision tickets** — questions whose resolution is a decision, not slices of a build to execute — one at a time until the route is clear.

The destination varies per effort, and naming it is the first act of charting — it shapes every ticket. It might be a spec to hand off and iterate on, a decision to lock before planning starts, or a change made in place like a data-structure migration. The map is domain-agnostic — engineering work, course content, whatever fits the shape.

## Plan, don't do

Wayfinder is **planning** by default: each ticket resolves a decision, and the map is done when the way is clear — nothing left to decide before someone goes and does the thing. The pull to just do the work is usually the signal you've reached the edge of the map and it's time to hand off. An effort can override this in its **Notes** — carrying execution into the map itself — but absent that, produce decisions, not deliverables.

## Refer by name

Every map and ticket is an issue, so it has a **name** — its title. In everything the human reads — narration, the map's Decisions-so-far — refer to it by that name, never by a bare id, number, or slug. A wall of `#42, #43, #44` is illegible; names read at a glance. The id and URL don't vanish — a name wraps its link — but they ride *inside* the name, never stand in for it.

## The Map

The map is a single issue on this repo's issue tracker, labelled `wayfinder:map` — the canonical artifact. Its tickets are child issues of the map.

The map is an **index**, not a store. It lists the decisions made and points at the tickets that hold their detail; a decision lives in exactly one place — its ticket — so the map never restates it, only gists it and links.

**Where the map, its child tickets, blocking, and frontier queries physically live is tracker-specific.** The issue tracker should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if not. Consult the tracker doc's "Wayfinding operations" section for how _this_ repo expresses them. If no tracker has been provided, default to the local-markdown tracker.

### The map body

The whole map at low resolution, loaded once per session. Open tickets are **not** listed — they are open child issues, found by query.

```markdown
## Destination

<what reaching the end of this map looks like — the spec, decision, or change this effort is finding its way to. One or two lines; every session orients to it before choosing a ticket.>

## Notes

<domain; skills every session should consult; standing preferences for this effort>

## Decisions so far

<!-- the index — one line per closed ticket: enough to judge relevance, then zoom the link for the detail the ticket holds -->

- [<closed ticket title>](link) — <one-line gist of the answer>

## Not yet specified

<!-- see "Fog of war": in-scope fog you can't ticket yet; graduates as the frontier advances -->

## Out of scope

<!-- see "Out of scope": work ruled beyond the destination; closed, never graduates -->
```

### Tickets

Each ticket is a **child issue** of the map; the tracker's issue id is its identity. Its body is the question, sized to one 100K token agent session:

```markdown
## Question

<the decision or investigation this ticket resolves>
```

Each ticket carries a `wayfinder:<type>` label — one of `research`, `prototype`, `grilling`, `task` (see [Ticket Types](#ticket-types)).

A session **claims** a ticket by assigning it to the dev driving the map, **first**, before any work, so concurrent sessions skip it. That assignee _is_ the claim: an open, unassigned ticket is unclaimed.

Blocking uses the tracker's **native** dependency relationship — essential because it renders the frontier _visually_ in the tracker's own UI, so the human sees what's takeable without opening the map. Only a tracker that lacks native blocking falls back to a body convention. A ticket is **unblocked** when every ticket blocking it is closed; the **frontier** is the open, unblocked, unclaimed children — the edge of the known.

The answer isn't part of the body — it's recorded on resolution (see [Work through the map](#work-through-the-map)). Assets created while resolving a ticket are linked from the issue, not pasted in.

## Ticket Types

Every ticket is either **HITL** — human in the loop, worked *with* a human who speaks for themselves — or **AFK**, driven by the agent alone. A HITL ticket only resolves through that live exchange; the agent never stands in for the human's side of it (a grilling agent that answers its own questions has broken this).

- **Research** (AFK): Reading documentation, third-party APIs, or local resources like knowledge bases to surface a fact a decision waits on. Resolved by a `/research` **subagent**. Use when knowledge outside the current working directory is required.
- **Prototype** (HITL): Raise the fidelity of the discussion by making a cheap, rough, concrete artifact to react to — an outline, a rough take, a stub, or UI/logic code via the /prototype skill. Links the prototype as an asset. Use when "how should it look" or "how should it behave" is the key question.
- **Grilling** (HITL): Conversation via the /grilling and /domain-modeling skills, one question at a time. The default case.
- **Task** (HITL or AFK): Manual work that must happen before a *decision* can be made — nothing to decide, prototype, or research, but the discussion is blocked until it's done. Signing up for a service so its API can be judged, provisioning access, moving data so its shape can be seen. This is the one type that *does* rather than decides — and it earns its place by unblocking a decision, not by delivering the destination. The agent drives it alone where it can (AFK); otherwise it hands the human a precise checklist (HITL). Resolved when the work is done; the answer records what was done and any resulting facts (credentials location, new URLs, row counts) later tickets depend on.

## Fog of war

The map is _deliberately_ incomplete: don't chart what you can't yet see. Beyond the live tickets lies the **fog of war** — the dim view of decisions and investigations you can tell are coming but can't yet pin down, because they hang on questions still open. Resolving a ticket clears the fog ahead of it, graduating whatever's now specifiable into fresh tickets — one at a time, until the way to the destination is clear and no tickets remain.

The map's **Not yet specified** section is where that dim view is written down: the suspected question, the area to revisit later. It's the undiscovered frontier _toward_ the destination — everything here is in scope, just not sharp enough to ticket. Write as loosely or as fully as the view allows; it doubles as a signpost for collaborators reading where the effort is headed.

**Fog or ticket?** The test is whether you can state the question precisely now — _not_ whether you can answer it now.

- **Ticket when** the question is already sharp — even if it's blocked and you can't act on it yet.
- **Not yet specified when** you can't yet phrase it that sharply. Don't pre-slice the fog into ticket-sized pieces: it's coarser than a ticket, and one patch may graduate into several tickets, or none, once the frontier reaches it.

**Not yet specified** excludes what's already decided (Decisions so far), what's already a live ticket, and what's out of scope (the next section).

## Out of scope

Fog only ever gathers _toward_ the destination. The destination fixes the scope, so work beyond it is **out of scope** — it isn't fog, and it doesn't belong in **Not yet specified**. It gets its own **Out of scope** section on the map: work you've consciously ruled out of _this_ effort. Scope, not sharpness, lands it here.

Out-of-scope work never graduates — the frontier stops at the destination — so it returns only if the destination is redrawn, and then as a fresh effort, not a resumption.

Ruling something out of scope is a scoping act, not a step on the route. When a ticket that already exists turns out to sit past the destination — mis-scoped in while charting, or exposed by a resolution — **close it** (a closed ticket is unambiguously off the frontier) and leave one line in the **Out of scope** section: the gist plus why it's out of scope, linking the closed ticket. It stays out of **Decisions so far**, which records the route actually walked — a scope boundary isn't a step on it.

## Invocation

Two modes. Either way, **never resolve more than one ticket per session** — with the exception of research tickets.

### Chart the map

User invokes with a loose idea.

1. **Name the destination.** Run a `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling` session to pin down what this map is finding its way to — the spec, decision, or change. The destination fixes the scope, so it's settled first.
2. **Map the frontier.** Grill again, **breadth-first** this time: fan out across the whole space rather than deep on any one thread, surfacing the open decisions and the first steps takeable now. **If this surfaces no fog** — the way to the destination is already clear, the whole journey small enough for one session — you don't need a map. Stop and ask the user how they'd like to proceed.
3. **Create the map** (label `wayfinder:map`): Destination and Notes filled in, Decisions-so-far empty, the fog sketched into **Not yet specified**.

Wiring sorts them into the frontier and the blocked; everything you can't yet specify stays in the fog — the **Not yet specified** section.
5. **Fire the research subagents.** For each `research` ticket you just created, spin up a `/research` subagent to resolve it in parallel, capturing its findings on a throwaway `research/<name>` branch with a context pointer from the ticket.

User invokes with a map (URL or number). A ticket is **optional** — without one, you pick the next decision, not the user.

1. Load the **map** — the low-res view, not every ticket body.
2. Choose the ticket. If the user named one, use it. Otherwise take the first frontier ticket in order. **Claim it**: assign it to yourself before any work.

=== MAP: Destination / Notes / Decisions (low-res) ===
wayfinder: the engine write plane — from user mutation to published record
## Destination

A settled design and a dependency-linked chain of build slices covering the engine's **write plane** end to end: from a user mutation entering `Engine::command` to a record published, registered, and readable by the resolve/read path landed in #811. Content bytes are one layer of that plane, not the whole of it.

The map is done when nothing is left to decide — the slices can be filed against #655 and built.

## Notes

**Domain:** `crates/engine` (write plane, content plane, sync/op-queue, net/publish), `crates/core` (content-seal primitive, envelope/read-body encode), the engine's hand-written API client, and the API's upload/registry/quota surface.

**Skills every session should consult:** `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling` by default; `/research` for the AFK research tickets; `/codebase-design` and `/design-an-interface` for the shared publish port.

**Standing preferences for this effort:**

- `CONTEXT.md` is the ubiquitous language — use its terms exactly (op queue, pending-op overlay, dead-letter, register-first, name inventory, advisory pin row, content key, adoption gate, floor law, eager set).
- `blueprint/core.md` and `blueprint/engine.md` are normative; where they name an "open edge" or "judgment", that is an unmade decision this map owns.
- AGENTS.md rule 8 (encode/decode fail-closed symmetry, release-active `Err`, never `debug_assert!`) and rule 7 (zeroize at the terminal owner only) bind every decision here.
- Determinism is injected — entropy, time, and policy enter as seam traits; never a direct clock or RNG.
- This is a **planning** map. It produces decisions and a slice chain, not the implementation.

**Scoping calls already made (2026-07-27):**

- Chunk size, DAG fan-out shape, and retention defaults are **in scope** — this effort freezes them, with an engine-side KAT vector for the DAG root block.
- The pin-provider layer ships **all three** `PinMode`s (Hosted, External, Dual), with the #705 advisory-quota fix folded in.
- The publish driver is **one shared port**, later backing rotation's `WriteWavePublisher` / `ScopeRootPublisher` (#635) — not a second register-first implementation.

## Why this map exists

Reconnaissance (2026-07-27) established that the gap is not content-specific. The engine has **no production write plane at all**:

- `sync::rebase::replay` (`crates/engine/src/sync/rebase.rs:138`) has no `src/` caller.
- `sync/tick.rs::run_tick_loop` (`crates/engine/src/sync/tick.rs:178`) has no `src/` caller.
- `seal_read_body` / `encode_envelope` appear in the engine only inside `#[cfg(test)]` modules.
- `ApiClient::upload` and `ApiClient::quota` (`crates/engine/src/api/client.rs:292`, `:283`) have zero production callers.
- The content plane's write half — `seal_content` (`content/mod.rs:86`), `frame_and_seal` (`content/chunk.rs:78`), `dag::assemble` (`content/dag.rs:106`) — is built and KAT-frozen in core, and entirely orphaned.

Consequence: today a plain `mkdir` stages an op, emits `SnapshotUpdated`, and publishes nothing — the op sits in the queue forever. `Create { content: None }` is not implemented either; it fails silently rather than returning `Unimplemented`.

## Decisions so far

<!-- one line per closed ticket -->

- [where does the upload boundary sit relative to the durable op journal?](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/814) — seal at command time, stage the sealed bytes, upload at drain. Ratified rather than chosen: `sync/staging.rs:40-42` and `sync/op.rs:11-13` already bind it, and the staging budget only has meaning if upload is deferred. Surfaced #828 (staged-blob shape) and the missing `EngineError::OverBudget` surface.

## Resolution

Answered from source and tests; no stack needed. Full note with citations:
`.planning/research/pin-row-ingress.md` on branch `research/pin-row-ingress`
(local only, commit 390ba4c35 — not pushed).

### 1. The three orderings

All three are safe. `uq_pinned_cids_account_cid` plus the SHARED per-CID advisory
lock — `content.service.ts:218-222` and `registry.service.ts:128` take the same
`advisoryLockKey(cid)` — make "no conflict, no duplicate" structural, and the two
paths are strictly serialized per CID.

- **upload → register**: register **no-ops** the pin row (filtered out via
  `knownCids`, `registry.service.ts:171-176`); it still writes the
  `name_inventory` row. Final `size = N`, `advisory = false`.
- **register → upload**: upload **promotes in place** — a size-0 registry row is
  deliberately NOT treated as a completed pin (`content.service.ts:250-277`), so
  the bytes get pinned and charged. Final `size = N`, `advisory = false`. An
  over-quota promote 413s before any pin and leaves the row at `size = '0'`; a
  post-commit pin failure reverts only the charge and keeps the registration.
- **register only, never uploaded**: row stays `size = '0'`, `advisory = user.byo`,
  indefinitely. Zero quota effect — but it **does hold a global refcount**, so a
  phantom registration keeps a CID pinned when the account that really uploaded it
  retires. Register also validates nothing about the CID string.

### 2. `sumHostedBytes` vs `sumPinnedBytes` — equal today, divergence is latent

They can only differ by `SUM(size) WHERE advisory = true`, and **no production
write path can produce a row with `advisory = true AND size > 0`**: `register` is
the only writer that sets `advisory = true` and it always writes `size = '0'`
(`registry.service.ts:176`); the only writers of a positive size stamp
`advisory = false` (`content.service.ts:275,279`); `setByo` does not rewrite
existing rows. So the two sums agree for every account reachable via the API, and
the pre-flight cannot disagree with the 413 *on this axis*. The existing
"divergence" test (`content.service.integration.test.ts:433-455`) hand-seeds a
state production cannot reach.

If the invariant ever breaks, the direction is `sumPinnedBytes > sumHostedBytes` —

## Summary

1. **Fan-out is NOT forward-compatible with `decode_root`** — the definitive answer the ticket asked for. Two independent hard rejects at `dag.rs:183-187` (every link must carry codec `0x55` raw; an interior node is `0x71`) and `dag.rs:188-192` (`links.len() == ceil(size/chunkSize)`). Plus a reader-side flat assumption in `leaf_range_for_byte_range`. Shipping flat is a real wire-format commitment, not a deferral.
2. Mitigating: it fails **closed and loud**, never a silent misread. Unknown map fields *are* tolerated (core codec #27 D10), so a later `v`/`height` field helps a future decoder dispatch — but old clients still can't read new-shape files.
3. **Flat capacity:** 110,375 max links under the 4 MiB cap (matches existing guard tests). Max file 26.95 GiB @256 KiB, 107.79 GiB @1 MiB. Flat is defensible for v2.0 on capacity.
4. **2 MiB chunks are unavailable** — they seal to 2 MiB + 40 B, over the Bitswap/trustless-gateway ecosystem ceiling. 1 MiB is the largest safe size.
5. **256 KiB has no published rationale** — IPIP-499 §3.2 says it was picked in the go-ipfs alpha and "never contested since". IPIP-499 moves the ecosystem *up* to 1 MiB / 1024 links.

content.text:
Facts established, and two of them correct the ticket's own framing:

**The API's 100 MiB cap is per *block*, not per file.** `ApiClient::upload` uploads one block per call (`client.rs:292`), and `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` gates a single raw request body (`app-setup.ts:8`). So it caps chunk size, which any sane value satisfies — it does not bound file size at all. The real file ceiling is the flat-DAG root cap (~108 GiB at 1 MiB chunks) and client memory.

**The copy amplification is per block, not per file.** `upload` does `content.to_vec()` (`client.rs:298`) and `request_authed` does `body.clone()` to keep a copy for the 401 retry (`client.rs:438-441`) — so ~3x, but of one *block*, bounded by chunk size. The ticket describes this as 3x of a 100 MiB payload; that's only true if the whole file went as one blob, which it doesn't.

Which means **option 3 in the ticket — giving the `Http` seam a streaming body — buys almost nothing.** The HTTP bodies are already chunk-sized. The memory problem is upstream of the wire, in the seal step.

Here's the actual peak, for a file of P bytes:

```
JS heap:    P            (File -> ArrayBuffer)
wasm heap:  P            (wasm_bindgen copies Vec<u8> in — lib.rs:401)
          + P + 40n      (frame_and_seal leaves; plaintext still alive)
          + S            (staged blob assembly, shape per #828)
```

roughly **4P** at peak. On wasm32 that lands against a 4 GiB address space with browsers OOMing well below it — and wasm linear memory does not shrink, so one large upload permanently inflates the worker's footprint for the session.

That reframes the fork. It isn't really "where does streaming go" — it's **does the whole plaintext ever exist in the wasm heap at once**, which surfaces a fourth option the ticket didn't list:

options.description: The facade command carries a content HANDLE, not bytes. The engine pulls chunk i on demand through a new seam, seals and stages each chunk incrementally, then journals one op. Peak memory becomes O(chunk) instead of O(4P), and it stays 'one journaled op regardless of online state'. Pairs naturally with #828 option D (key per block). Costs a new seam trait, a wasm binding change from Vec<u8> to a handle, and a trivial desktop impl. Recommended.

options.label: Full in-memory Vec<u8>
options.description: Keep today's shape (wasm lib.rs:401 takes Vec<u8>). Simplest, no seam change, and #828 option A follows. Accepts ~4P peak and a stated max file size in the low hundreds of MiB in a browser tab, plus permanent worker footprint growth after a large upload.

content.text:
Noted — client slices and feeds chunks. That keeps the plaintext in the JS heap where the `File` already lives and never materializes it in wasm, without inventing a pull seam. It does leave two things to settle, and this is the sharper one.

The tension I flagged is resolvable: the engine can still **own** framing policy (the chunk size, per `engine.md:483-487`) while the client does the mechanical slicing — the engine tells the client what size to slice at. That's a policy/mechanism split, not a violation.

What doesn't resolve itself is journaling. `stage_op` is fail-closed on exactly this: a content op carrying a staging key with no bytes is "a broken caller contract" that must never journal (`staging.rs:71-76`). A multi-call push means there's a window where chunks exist but the op doesn't — or worse, the reverse.

questions.question: With the client pushing chunks across multiple calls, when is the op journaled?

options.label: Stage-then-commit
options.description: Client opens a write, pushes chunks (engine seals and stages each as it arrives), then calls commit — and only then is the single op journaled, atomically, referencing already-complete staged bytes. Preserves stage_op's fail-closed invariant untouched and keeps 'one journaled op'. A crash mid-push leaves staged bytes with no op, which orphan_staging_keys already GCs by construction. Recommended.
options.preview:
beginWrite(node) -> WriteHandle { chunkSize }
pushChunk(handle, bytes)      // seal + stage, repeat
commitWrite(handle)           // ONE op journaled here

crash mid-push -> staged bytes, no op -> orphan GC
stage_op invariant (staging.rs:71-76) unchanged

options.label: Journal first, append after
options.description: Op is journaled up front, chunks appended to its staging key as they arrive. Means a durable op can reference incomplete content, which is exactly what staging.rs:71-76 fails closed on today — that invariant would have to be relaxed, and a crash mid-push leaves a queued op pointing at a truncated version.

options.label: One call, client pre-slices
options.description: Client slices but still hands the whole array of chunks in a single facade call. No protocol change and no window at all — but every chunk crosses into wasm at once, which reintroduces the O(P) heap cost the choice was meant to avoid.

content.text:
Here's the full rundown. Let P = plaintext bytes, n = chunk count.

| | A: stage-then-commit | B: journal first, append | C: one call, pre-sliced |
|---|---|---|---|
| Peak wasm heap | O(chunk) | O(chunk) | **O(P)** |
| `staging.rs:71-76` invariant | untouched | **must be relaxed** | untouched |
| Crash mid-write | orphan bytes, GC'd | **truncated version, publishable** | nothing staged |
| Budget fail-fast | needs declared size | needs declared size | native |
| New facade surface | 3 commands + handle | 3 commands + handle | none |
| Content key lifetime | held across push | held across push | single call |
| Forces #828 choice | **yes — option D** | yes — option D | any |
| Touches landed code | `stage_op` split | `stage_op` split + invariant | none |
| Fits desktop FUSE | **well** | well | poorly |

**C is not actually viable, and I should say so plainly.** If the client hands an array of N chunks in one call, `wasm_bindgen` copies all of them across at once — peak wasm heap is O(P) again. It's the full-in-memory model with extra steps, so it contradicts the decision you already made in this ticket. I listed it for completeness; it doesn't survive contact with the memory constraint.

**B has a silent-corruption mode.** With the op journaled up front and chunks appended after, a crash mid-push leaves a queued op referencing a *prefix* of the file. The drain driver would publish that as a complete version — a file silently truncated, with a valid CID, that passes every read-path check because it's internally consistent. Detecting it needs a completeness marker, which is extra durable state that exists only to patch a hazard A doesn't have. And `staging.rs:71-76` fails closed on precisely this shape today, so B means deleting an existing safety property.

**A's costs are higher than I first implied, and two are worth naming:**

*It forces #828's hand.* `put_staged_bytes` **replaces** the bytes at a key (`seams/staging_store.rs:38`) — there is no append. So staging chunks incrementally into one blob would mean read-modify-write of the whole blob per chunk: O(P²) I/O. A therefore forces per-block staging keys, i.e. #828 option D, which in turn forces the `orphan_staging_keys` rework. Those two tickets are no longer independent.

*It puts stateful handles into a command/event facade.* `Command` is currently a clean one-shot intent enum (`facade.rs:235-350`). `beginWrite`/`pushChunk`/`commitWrite` introduces session state with a lifetime, plus a live content key held in memory per open handle for the duration (`chunk.rs:18-22` — one key seals every chunk of a version), with rule-7 zeroization discipline on each. That's a genuine architectural shift, not just three more variants.

**Two things that cut in A's favour beyond memory:**

*Budget fail-fast is recoverable.* Checking the budget per `pushChunk` would turn fail-fast into fail-midway, with partial staging to roll back. But the client knows `File.size` up front, so `beginWrite` can declare the total and check it against remaining budget before a single byte is sealed — fail-fast preserved, arguably cleaner than today's.

*It fits desktop.* FUSE writes arrive as offset/length calls (#647–#650), so a push protocol matches how the desktop write path will actually receive data. A one-shot command would force desktop to buffer whole files just to hand them back chunk-wise.

So on the evidence the live choice is A or B, and B trades a safety property for nothing A doesn't already provide.

questions.question: With that rundown, when is the op journaled?

options.label: Stage-then-commit (A)
options.description: One op journaled at commit, referencing complete staged bytes. Keeps the fail-closed invariant, makes crash-mid-write a clean no-op, and fits the desktop FUSE write path. Accepts stateful handles in the facade, a stage_op split, and forces #828 to option D. Recommended — B's only advantage over it is avoiding those costs, at the price of a silently-truncatable version.

options.label: Journal first, append (B)
options.description: Op journaled up front. Requires relaxing staging.rs:71-76, adding a durable completeness marker to avoid publishing truncated versions, and handling rebase against an op whose content is still arriving.

options.label: Reopen the memory choice
options.description: The commit-protocol cost is high enough that the pull-based content source seam, or the full in-memory model, is worth reconsidering before committing to a push protocol. Reopens the earlier answer in this ticket rather than building on it.

Part of #813

## Question

What should `SyncTimingProfile::PRODUCTION.staging_budget_bytes` be, measured against real durable-storage limits on every host?

## Why this is now load-bearing

#815 resolved that the client slices and feeds chunks, with a stage-then-commit protocol. Under that model the **entire sealed file sits in the staging store until drain completes**, so the staging budget *is* the maximum uploadable file size. Every other candidate ceiling is an order of magnitude away:

- wasm heap — now O(chunk), bounds nothing
- flat-DAG root cap — 110,375 links, so 107.79 GiB at a 1 MiB chunk size
- API `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` — 100 MiB **per block**, not per file

The current value is `1 << 30` (1 GiB) at `crates/engine/src/profile.rs:59`, and `profile.rs:49` explicitly calls it "a placeholder pending the measurement". So the shipped answer to "how large a file can CipherBox store" is currently an unvalidated constant.

## What to establish

1. **Web** — practical durable-storage limits for OPFS and IndexedDB across Chrome, Firefox, and Safari: how quota is computed (share of free disk, per-origin caps), what `navigator.storage.estimate()` actually reports, and what happens on quota exhaustion mid-write. Note whether persistent storage permission changes the ceiling and whether eviction can reclaim staged bytes under storage pressure — staged bytes being evicted mid-flight would be a durability hazard worth naming.
2. **Desktop** — the local-journal equivalent, and whether the same budget number makes sense on a host with ordinary filesystem access. A single shared constant may be wrong across platforms.
3. Whether the budget should be a **fixed constant or a fraction of available quota** measured at runtime, and if the latter, what seam surfaces it (determinism rules say it enters as a parameter, never a direct query from core logic).
4. What the user-visible behaviour is when a file exceeds the budget: `stage_op` returns `RejectedOverBudget { staged, incoming, budget }` today (`sync/staging.rs:61-65`), and #814 established the facade needs a typed `EngineError::OverBudget` to surface it. Establish what number the UI should quote.
5. Whether concurrent uploads sharing one budget needs a per-op reservation, given a stage-then-commit push can now occupy budget for a long window.

Note the drain can `remove_staged_bytes` per block as it uploads (per-block staging keys, #828), so the budget frees incrementally during drain rather than all at once — factor that into the sizing.

## Method

Primary sources: the Storage Standard, MDN storage-quota documentation, and browser-vendor docs on eviction policy. Prefer specs and vendor documentation over blog posts; cite URLs. Capture findings as a research note and link it here.

input.content:
## Resolution

**The client slices the `File` and feeds chunks; the engine seals and stages each as it arrives; the op is journaled once, at commit.**

### Memory model

Plaintext stays in the JS heap where the `File` already lives and is never materialized whole in wasm. Peak wasm heap is O(chunk) rather than the ~4P a one-shot command incurs:

```
JS heap:    P            File -> ArrayBuffer
wasm heap:  P            wasm_bindgen copies Vec<u8> in   (crates/wasm/src/lib.rs:401)
          + P + 40n      frame_and_seal leaves, plaintext still alive
          + S            staged blob assembly
```

The engine still **owns framing policy** — it dictates the chunk size per `blueprint/engine.md:483-487`; the client performs only the mechanical slicing. Policy/mechanism split, not a transfer of ownership.

### Commit protocol: stage-then-commit

`beginWrite` (declaring total size) → repeated `pushChunk` (seal + stage each) → `commitWrite`, which journals the single op against already-complete staged bytes. This keeps `stage_op`'s fail-closed invariant intact — a content op carrying a staging key with no bytes remains "a broken caller contract" (`sync/staging.rs:71-76`) — and preserves "one journaled op regardless of online state" (`engine.md:208-211`).

Crash mid-push leaves staged bytes with no op, which `orphan_staging_keys` already GCs by construction (`staging.rs:88-111`). The write simply did not happen, which is the correct semantics.

Rejected: **journal-first-then-append**, because a crash mid-push would leave a queued op referencing a *prefix* of the file, which the drain would publish as a complete, internally-consistent, silently-truncated version. Detecting that needs a durable completeness marker that exists only to patch a hazard stage-then-commit does not have — and it would mean deleting an existing safety property.

Rejected: **one call with a pre-sliced array**, because `wasm_bindgen` copies every chunk across at once, returning peak heap to O(P). It is the full-in-memory model with extra steps.

Also noted: giving the `Http` seam a streaming body (the ticket's candidate 3) buys almost nothing. `ApiClient::upload` sends one block per call (`api/client.rs:292`), so HTTP bodies are already chunk-sized; the memory cost was upstream, at the seal step.

### Max file size

**The staging budget is the answer** — under stage-then-commit the whole sealed file occupies staging until drain completes. Every other ceiling is an order of magnitude away:

| Bound | Value |
| --- | --- |
| **Staging budget** | **`1 << 30` = 1 GiB** (`profile.rs:59`) |
| Flat-DAG root cap | 107.79 GiB at 1 MiB chunks (110,375 links under the 4 MiB cap) |
| API `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` | 100 MiB **per block**, not per file |
| wasm heap | O(chunk) — bounds nothing |

Two corrections to this ticket's own framing, for the record: the API's 100 MiB cap is per-block and does **not** bound file size, and the `content.to_vec()` / `body.clone()` amplification (`client.rs:298`, `:438-441`) is ~3x of one *block*, not of a 100 MiB payload.

`profile.rs:49` calls the budget "a placeholder pending the measurement", so the shipped max file size is currently an unvalidated constant. Filed as #829 (research), which now blocks the format freeze #820.

## Consequences for other tickets

- **#828 (staged blob shape) is forced to option D — one staging key per block.** `put_staged_bytes` *replaces* the bytes at a key (`seams/staging_store.rs:38`); there is no append. Staging incrementally into a single blob would mean read-modify-write of the whole blob per chunk, i.e. O(P²) I/O. Per-block keys follow, and with them the `orphan_staging_keys` rework.
- **`stage_op` must be split** into "stage bytes" and "enqueue op" as separate steps, since staging now happens across many calls before the single journaling step. Landed, tested code.
- **The facade gains stateful handles.** `Command` is a one-shot intent enum today (`facade.rs:235-350`); a write handle carries session state plus a live per-version content key held in memory for the push duration (`content/chunk.rs:18-22` — one key seals every chunk of a version), under rule-7 zeroization discipline. Feeds #818 and #824.
- **Budget fail-fast is preserved** by declaring total size at `beginWrite` rather than checking per chunk, which would turn fail-fast into fail-midway with partial staging to unwind.
- **Drain frees budget incrementally**, calling `remove_staged_bytes` per block as it uploads.
- **Desktop benefits**: FUSE writes arrive as offset/length calls (#647–#650), so a push protocol matches how the desktop write path receives data natively.

name: feedback-nested-subagents-share-worktree-clobber
description: "A nested helper shares the parent agent's worktree checkout — its git checkout/fmt can clobber the parent's uncommitted WIP"

When a background implementation agent (in an `isolation:worktree` worktree) spawns a NESTED sub-agent to build part of the same slice, the child shares the PARENT'S single worktree checkout — they do NOT get separate checkouts. If both edit concurrently, a child's `git checkout HEAD`/`git restore`/`git stash`/`cargo fmt --all`/cp-restore can silently CLOBBER or reformat the parent's UNCOMMITTED WIP (observed on #635 Slice 1: a child index-builder reverted the parent's grant-section gate/seal edits).

**Why:** worktree isolation is per-top-level-agent, not per-nested-agent. Uncommitted edits are the vulnerable surface. See [[feedback-background-agents-can-nest-subagents]] and [[feedback-manager-plan-inline-not-background-shared-checkout]].

**How to apply:** when briefing a big-slice agent that may fan out nested helpers, require it to (a) COMMIT its own WIP before delegating any concurrent file-touching sub-task, (b) give each nested helper a DISJOINT file set, (c) forbid destructive git (`checkout HEAD`/`restore`/`stash`) and `cargo fmt --all` in a shared checkout while a sibling is live, and (d) reconcile from its own context — never trust on-disk state — if a collision is reported. Prefer serial sub-tasks over concurrent ones in one worktree. Recovery: the file-owning agent re-applies its edits from context, re-validates the integrated tree, then commits promptly.

---
name: feedback-sibling-bg-agents-clobber-branch-refs
description: "Concurrent sibling background agents share the MAIN checkout — their git checkout -b + commit sequences interleave, so commits land on the wrong branch and one branch ends up empty"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
---

Two background agents launched in parallel from the same session (NOT `isolation:worktree`) share the session's single main checkout. If each is told to "create branch `research/<name>` and commit your file there", their `git checkout -b` / `git add` / `git commit` sequences interleave: agent B branches off whatever HEAD agent A has just committed, so B's branch contains BOTH commits, and A's branch ref can be left pointing at plain `main` with **nothing on it**. The checkout is also left on a random research branch instead of `main`.

Observed 2026-07-27 (wayfinder map #813): `research/pin-row-ingress` ended up empty while `research/content-format-freeze` carried both notes; the pin-row agent even reported the anomaly itself ("a concurrent sibling agent committed onto this branch").

**Why:** worktree isolation is opt-in per agent. Without it, "parallel agents" are parallel only in reasoning — they serialize destructively over one working tree and one HEAD. Distinct from [[feedback-nested-subagents-share-worktree-clobber]], which is about a nested helper clobbering the parent's *uncommitted* WIP; this one corrupts *branch refs and commit topology* between siblings.

**How to apply:** when fanning out concurrent agents that must each produce a git artifact, either (a) give each `isolation: "worktree"`, or (b) have them write their file and NOT commit, leaving the commits to the orchestrator serially, or (c) brief each to branch off `main` explicitly (`git checkout -b <name> main`) and verify with `git log --oneline -3` that its commit sits directly on a main commit. Always verify afterwards with `git ls-tree -r --name-only <branch> -- <path>` per branch — an agent reporting success is not evidence its branch holds the file. Recovery is cheap and non-destructive: `git branch -f <branch> <its-commit-sha>` repoints the empty branch; the commit is still reachable from the sibling's branch. Do not switch branches in the shared checkout while another agent is still running.

Session done. Two research tickets settled and one grilling ticket resolved — the cap allows research tickets on top of the one decision.

**[The memory model](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/815) — resolved.** Client slices the `File` and feeds chunks; the engine seals and stages each, retaining framing *policy* (it dictates chunk size, client does the mechanical slicing); the op is journaled once at commit. Peak wasm heap drops from ~4P to O(chunk). Journal-first-then-append was rejected because a crash mid-push would publish a silently truncated but internally-consistent version, and it would mean deleting the `staging.rs:71-76` safety property; the pre-sliced-array variant was rejected because `wasm_bindgen` copies every chunk at once, which is the full-in-memory model with extra steps.

Two corrections to the ticket's own framing went into the record: the API's 100 MiB cap is **per block**, not per file, and the copy amplification is 3x of one block, not of the payload. Which also means giving the `Http` seam a streaming body — the ticket's third candidate — buys nearly nothing.

**Max file size = the staging budget**, `1 << 30` = 1 GiB (`profile.rs:59`), an explicitly unmeasured placeholder. Everything else is an order of magnitude off: flat-DAG ceiling 107.79 GiB, wasm now unbounded-by-heap. Filed [the staging budget measurement](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/829) as research, blocking the format freeze, and its agent is running.

**Knock-on effects recorded:** [the staged blob shape](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/828) is now *forced* to per-block keys — `put_staged_bytes` replaces rather than appends, so incremental staging into one blob would be O(P²) I/O. `stage_op` must split into stage-bytes and enqueue-op. The facade gains stateful write handles, which feeds the content-key and cancel tickets. Desktop benefits: FUSE writes arrive as offset/length calls, so a push protocol matches natively.

**[Chunk size and DAG shape](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/816) — research closed.** Fan-out is definitively **not** forward-compatible with `decode_root`, so flat is a genuine wire-format commitment (though it fails closed and loud, never silently). 2 MiB chunks are unavailable — they seal to 2 MiB + 40 B, over the trustless-gateway ceiling — making 1 MiB the largest safe size, and 256 KiB turns out to have no published rationale. Undocumented finding: fresh per-version content keys mean **zero cross-version leaf dedup by construction**, so keep-all retention costs k × filesize.

**One thing you should know about:** the two parallel research agents shared the main checkout and clobbered each other. `research/pin-row-ingress` ended up **empty** while `research/content-format-freeze` carried both notes, and the checkout was left on a research branch rather than `main`. I repointed the branch with `git branch -f` (non-destructive — the commit was still reachable) and verified both branches now hold exactly their own file. I did *not* switch branches, since the budget agent is live in that same checkout. Saved as a memory, since it's a different failure mode from the nested-agent one already recorded: siblings corrupt branch refs, not uncommitted WIP.

**Frontier is now 6:** [content key custody](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/818), [ordering and rollback](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/819) (unblocked by the pin-row research), [read-after-write](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/817), [pin-provider layer](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/822), [cancel semantics](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/824), and [staged blob shape](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/828) — the last of which is now nearly mechanical, since its answer is forced.
