---
name: feedback-nested-subagents-share-worktree-clobber
description: "A nested helper shares the parent agent's worktree checkout — its git checkout/fmt can clobber the parent's uncommitted WIP"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: af9d085f-d8ee-4c7c-a115-037957347414
  modified: 2026-07-27T14:06:38.840Z
---

When a background implementation agent (in an `isolation:worktree` worktree) spawns a NESTED sub-agent to build part of the same slice, the child shares the PARENT'S single worktree checkout — they do NOT get separate checkouts. If both edit concurrently, a child's `git checkout HEAD`/`git restore`/`git stash`/`cargo fmt --all`/cp-restore can silently CLOBBER or reformat the parent's UNCOMMITTED WIP (observed on #635 Slice 1: a child index-builder reverted the parent's grant-section gate/seal edits).

**Why:** worktree isolation is per-top-level-agent, not per-nested-agent. Uncommitted edits are the vulnerable surface. See [[feedback-background-agents-can-nest-subagents]] and [[feedback-manager-plan-inline-not-background-shared-checkout]]. The sibling-agent analogue, which corrupts branch refs rather than uncommitted WIP, is [[feedback-sibling-bg-agents-clobber-branch-refs]].

**How to apply:** when briefing a big-slice agent that may fan out nested helpers, require it to (a) COMMIT its own WIP before delegating any concurrent file-touching sub-task, (b) give each nested helper a DISJOINT file set, (c) forbid destructive git (`checkout HEAD`/`restore`/`stash`) and `cargo fmt --all` in a shared checkout while a sibling is live, and (d) reconcile from its own context — never trust on-disk state — if a collision is reported. Prefer serial sub-tasks over concurrent ones in one worktree. Recovery: the file-owning agent re-applies its edits from context, re-validates the integrated tree, then commits promptly.

---
name: feedback-sibling-bg-agents-clobber-branch-refs
description: "Concurrent sibling background agents share the MAIN checkout — their git checkout -b + commit sequences interleave, so commits land on the wrong branch and one branch ends up empty"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 8267f28c-a642-4499-8ed8-0ab37af2bee1
  modified: 2026-07-27T14:06:30.402Z
---

Two background agents launched in parallel from the same session (NOT `isolation:worktree`) share the session's single main checkout. If each is told to "create branch `research/<name>` and commit your file there", their `git checkout -b` / `git add` / `git commit` sequences interleave: agent B branches off whatever HEAD agent A has just committed, so B's branch contains BOTH commits, and A's branch ref can be left pointing at plain `main` with **nothing on it**. The checkout is also left on a random research branch instead of `main`.

Observed 2026-07-27 (wayfinder map #813): `research/pin-row-ingress` ended up empty while `research/content-format-freeze` carried both notes; the pin-row agent even reported the anomaly itself ("a concurrent sibling agent committed onto this branch").

**Why:** worktree isolation is opt-in per agent. Without it, "parallel agents" are parallel only in reasoning — they serialize destructively over one working tree and one HEAD. Distinct from [[feedback-nested-subagents-share-worktree-clobber]], which is about a nested helper clobbering the parent's *uncommitted* WIP; this one corrupts *branch refs and commit topology* between siblings.

**How to apply:** when fanning out concurrent agents that must each produce a git artifact, either (a) give each `isolation: "worktree"`, or (b) have them write their file and NOT commit, leaving the commits to the orchestrator serially, or (c) brief each to branch off `main` explicitly (`git checkout -b <name> main`) and verify with `git log --oneline -3` that its commit sits directly on a main commit. Always verify afterwards with `git ls-tree -r --name-only <branch> -- <path>` per branch — an agent reporting success is not evidence its branch holds the file. Recovery is cheap and non-destructive: `git branch -f <branch> <its-commit-sha>` repoints the empty branch; the commit is still reachable from the sibling's branch. Do not switch branches in the shared checkout while another agent is still running.

## Resolution

**The client slices the `File` and feeds chunks; the engine seals and stages each as it arrives; the op is journaled once, at commit.**

### Memory model

Plaintext stays in the JS heap where the `File` already lives and is never materialized whole in wasm. Peak wasm heap is O(chunk) rather than the ~4P a one-shot command incurs:

```
JS heap:    P            File -> ArrayBuffer
wasm heap:  P            wasm_bindgen copies Vec<u8> in   (crates/wasm/src/lib.rs:401)
          + P + 40n      frame_and_seal leaves, plaintext still alive
          + S            staged blob assembly
```

The engine still **owns framing policy** — it dictates the chunk size per `blueprint/engine.md:483-487`; the client performs only the mechanical slicing. Policy/mechanism split, not a transfer of ownership.

### Commit protocol: stage-then-commit

`beginWrite` (declaring total size) → repeated `pushChunk` (seal + stage each) → `commitWrite`, which journals the single op against already-complete staged bytes. This keeps `stage_op`'s fail-closed invariant intact — a content op carrying a staging key with no bytes remains "a broken caller contract" (`sync/staging.rs:71-76`) — and preserves "one journaled op regardless of online state" (`engine.md:208-211`).

Crash mid-push leaves staged bytes with no op, which `orphan_staging_keys` already GCs by construction (`staging.rs:88-111`). The write simply did not happen, which is the correct semantics.

Rejected: **journal-first-then-append**, because a crash mid-push would leave a queued op referencing a *prefix* of the file, which the drain would publish as a complete, internally-consistent, silently-truncated version. Detecting that needs a durable completeness marker that exists only to patch a hazard stage-then-commit does not have — and it would mean deleting an existing safety property.

Rejected: **one call with a pre-sliced array**, because `wasm_bindgen` copies every chunk across at once, returning peak heap to O(P). It is the full-in-memory model with extra steps.

Also noted: giving the `Http` seam a streaming body (the ticket's candidate 3) buys almost nothing. `ApiClient::upload` sends one block per call (`api/client.rs:292`), so HTTP bodies are already chunk-sized; the memory cost was upstream, at the seal step.

### Max file size

**The staging budget is the answer** — under stage-then-commit the whole sealed file occupies staging until drain completes. Every other ceiling is an order of magnitude away:

| Bound | Value |
| --- | --- |
| **Staging budget** | **`1 << 30` = 1 GiB** (`profile.rs:59`) |
| Flat-DAG root cap | 107.79 GiB at 1 MiB chunks (110,375 links under the 4 MiB cap) |
| API `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` | 100 MiB **per block**, not per file |
| wasm heap | O(chunk) — bounds nothing |

Two corrections to this ticket's own framing, for the record: the API's 100 MiB cap is per-block and does **not** bound file size, and the `content.to_vec()` / `body.clone()` amplification (`client.rs:298`, `:438-441`) is ~3x of one *block*, not of a 100 MiB payload.

`profile.rs:49` calls the budget "a placeholder pending the measurement", so the shipped max file size is currently an unvalidated constant. Filed as #829 (research), which now blocks the format freeze #820.

## Consequences for other tickets

- **#828 (staged blob shape) is forced to option D — one staging key per block.** `put_staged_bytes` *replaces* the bytes at a key (`seams/staging_store.rs:38`); there is no append. Staging incrementally into a single blob would mean read-modify-write of the whole blob per chunk, i.e. O(P²) I/O. Per-block keys follow, and with them the `orphan_staging_keys` rework.
- **`stage_op` must be split** into "stage bytes" and "enqueue op" as separate steps, since staging now happens across many calls before the single journaling step. Landed, tested code.
- **The facade gains stateful handles.** `Command` is a one-shot intent enum today (`facade.rs:235-350`); a write handle carries session state plus a live per-version content key held in memory for the push duration (`content/chunk.rs:18-22` — one key seals every chunk of a version), under rule-7 zeroization discipline. Feeds #818 and #824.
- **Budget fail-fast is preserved** by declaring total size at `beginWrite` rather than checking per chunk, which would turn fail-fast into fail-midway with partial staging to unwind.
- **Drain frees budget incrementally**, calling `remove_staged_bytes` per block as it uploads.
- **Desktop benefits**: FUSE writes arrive as offset/length calls (#647–#650), so a push protocol matches how the desktop write path receives data natively.

Part of #813

## Question

What should `SyncTimingProfile::PRODUCTION.staging_budget_bytes` be, measured against real durable-storage limits on every host?

## Why this is now load-bearing

#815 resolved that the client slices and feeds chunks, with a stage-then-commit protocol. Under that model the **entire sealed file sits in the staging store until drain completes**, so the staging budget *is* the maximum uploadable file size. Every other candidate ceiling is an order of magnitude away:

- wasm heap — now O(chunk), bounds nothing
- flat-DAG root cap — 110,375 links, so 107.79 GiB at a 1 MiB chunk size
- API `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` — 100 MiB **per block**, not per file

The current value is `1 << 30` (1 GiB) at `crates/engine/src/profile.rs:59`, and `profile.rs:49` explicitly calls it "a placeholder pending the measurement". So the shipped answer to "how large a file can CipherBox store" is currently an unvalidated constant.

## What to establish

1. **Web** — practical durable-storage limits for OPFS and IndexedDB across Chrome, Firefox, and Safari: how quota is computed (share of free disk, per-origin caps), what `navigator.storage.estimate()` actually reports, and what happens on quota exhaustion mid-write. Note whether persistent storage permission changes the ceiling and whether eviction can reclaim staged bytes under storage pressure — staged bytes being evicted mid-flight would be a durability hazard worth naming.
2. **Desktop** — the local-journal equivalent, and whether the same budget number makes sense on a host with ordinary filesystem access. A single shared constant may be wrong across platforms.
3. Whether the budget should be a **fixed constant or a fraction of available quota** measured at runtime, and if the latter, what seam surfaces it (determinism rules say it enters as a parameter, never a direct query from core logic).
4. What the user-visible behaviour is when a file exceeds the budget: `stage_op` returns `RejectedOverBudget { staged, incoming, budget }` today (`sync/staging.rs:61-65`), and #814 established the facade needs a typed `EngineError::OverBudget` to surface it. Establish what number the UI should quote.
5. Whether concurrent uploads sharing one budget needs a per-op reservation, given a stage-then-commit push can now occupy budget for a long window.

Note the drain can `remove_staged_bytes` per block as it uploads (per-block staging keys, #828), so the budget frees incrementally during drain rather than all at once — factor that into the sizing.

## Method

Primary sources: the Storage Standard, MDN storage-quota documentation, and browser-vendor docs on eviction policy. Prefer specs and vendor documentation over blog posts; cite URLs. Capture findings as a research note and link it here.

## Resolution

**Candidate 1: seal at command time, stage the sealed bytes, upload at drain.**

This is ratified rather than freshly chosen — the landed code already binds it in contract text, and the ticket's three-way framing was wrong to treat it as open:

- `sync/staging.rs:40-42` — "`upload` is the **already-sealed** content payload (core's content-seal runs upstream in the content plane); no plaintext user content ever lands in the staging store at rest." Sealing therefore happens before staging, i.e. inside `Engine::command`.
- `sync/op.rs:11-13` — "Content bytes never live in an op … the bytes sit in the staging store behind the profile budget."
- The staging budget (`SyncTimingProfile::staging_budget_bytes`, enforced at `staging.rs:54-70`) exists specifically so an **offline** device can stage an upload, which only has meaning if upload is deferred past the journal.

Candidate 2 (seal and upload eagerly, journal CIDs) is excluded: it would break the offline parity `blueprint/engine.md:208-211` and `web-client.md:189-193` require — "one journaled op regardless of online state". Candidate 3 (hybrid, upload eagerly when online) collapses with it and is rejected explicitly: two code paths for one op, with no offline guarantee bought.

## Consequences to carry into the slice chain

**The over-budget error surface must be designed with the command.** `stage_and_notify` (`facade.rs:1581-1597`) currently hardcodes `upload = None` and maps `StageOutcome::RejectedOverBudget` onto an internal `EngineError::Seam`. There is no `EngineError::OverBudget` variant (`facade.rs:449-512`), so the law that "past the budget only new uploads fail fast, while metadata ops queue unbounded" (`engine.md:233-235`, restated at `staging.rs:5-9`) is currently unexpressible at the facade boundary. A content-bearing `Create`/`UpdateContent` needs a typed over-budget error carrying `{staged, incoming, budget}`, distinct from a seam failure.

**A drain uploads N+1 times.** `ApiClient::upload` takes one blob and returns one `UploadResult { cid, size }` (`api/client.rs:292-303`), so every leaf plus the root is a separate call. This is an input to the ordering-and-rollback question (#819): a partial upload is the common case, not an edge case.

## Newly surfaced

Establishing the above exposed a sharper question the ticket did not anticipate: `SealedContent` is a root block plus N leaf blocks, but the staging store holds one opaque blob under one key and an `Op` carries exactly one `content_staging_key`. Filed as #828 with the full candidate comparison, blocked by #815 — the memory model determines the answer, so deciding the blob shape first would prejudge it from the wrong end.

## Still open, deliberately

Where the per-version content key lives across the durable boundary is **not** answered here — that is #818, which this ticket unblocks. Candidate 1 is what makes it hard: the key is a KDF non-edge (`crates/core/src/kdf/mod.rs:18-20`), so it cannot be re-derived, and something must carry it from command to drain.

skills.name: wayfinder
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/myankelev/.claude/skills/wayfinder

A loose idea has arrived — too big for one agent session, and wrapped in fog: the way from here to the **destination** isn't visible yet. Wayfinding is about finding that way, not charging at the destination. This skill charts the way as a **shared map** on the repo's issue tracker, then works its **decision tickets** — questions whose resolution is a decision, not slices of a build to execute — one at a time until the route is clear.

The destination varies per effort, and naming it is the first act of charting — it shapes every ticket. It might be a spec to hand off and iterate on, a decision to lock before planning starts, or a change made in place like a data-structure migration. The map is domain-agnostic — engineering work, course content, whatever fits the shape.

## Plan, don't do

Wayfinder is **planning** by default: each ticket resolves a decision, and the map is done when the way is clear — nothing left to decide before someone goes and does the thing. The pull to just do the work is usually the signal you've reached the edge of the map and it's time to hand off. An effort can override this in its **Notes** — carrying execution into the map itself — but absent that, produce decisions, not deliverables.

## Refer by name

Every map and ticket is an issue, so it has a **name** — its title. In everything the human reads — narration, the map's Decisions-so-far — refer to it by that name, never by a bare id, number, or slug. A wall of `#42, #43, #44` is illegible; names read at a glance. The id and URL don't vanish — a name wraps its link — but they ride *inside* the name, never stand in for it.

## The Map

The map is a single issue on this repo's issue tracker, labelled `wayfinder:map` — the canonical artifact. Its tickets are child issues of the map.

The map is an **index**, not a store. It lists the decisions made and points at the tickets that hold their detail; a decision lives in exactly one place — its ticket — so the map never restates it, only gists it and links.

**Where the map, its child tickets, blocking, and frontier queries physically live is tracker-specific.** The issue tracker should have been provided to you — run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if not. Consult the tracker doc's "Wayfinding operations" section for how _this_ repo expresses them. If no tracker has been provided, default to the local-markdown tracker.

### The map body

The whole map at low resolution, loaded once per session. Open tickets are **not** listed — they are open child issues, found by query.

```markdown
## Destination

<what reaching the end of this map looks like — the spec, decision, or change this effort is finding its way to. One or two lines; every session orients to it before choosing a ticket.>

## Notes

<domain; skills every session should consult; standing preferences for this effort>

## Decisions so far

<!-- the index — one line per closed ticket: enough to judge relevance, then zoom the link for the detail the ticket holds -->

- [<closed ticket title>](link) — <one-line gist of the answer>

## Not yet specified

<!-- see "Fog of war": in-scope fog you can't ticket yet; graduates as the frontier advances -->

## Out of scope

<!-- see "Out of scope": work ruled beyond the destination; closed, never graduates -->
```

### Tickets

Each ticket is a **child issue** of the map; the tracker's issue id is its identity. Its body is the question, sized to one 100K token agent session:

```markdown
## Question

<the decision or investigation this ticket resolves>
```

Each ticket carries a `wayfinder:<type>` label — one of `research`, `prototype`, `grilling`, `task` (see [Ticket Types](#ticket-types)).

A session **claims** a ticket by assigning it to the dev driving the map, **first**, before any work, so concurrent sessions skip it. That assignee _is_ the claim: an open, unassigned ticket is unclaimed.

Blocking uses the tracker's **native** dependency relationship — essential because it renders the frontier _visually_ in the tracker's own UI, so the human sees what's takeable without opening the map. Only a tracker that lacks native blocking falls back to a body convention. A ticket is **unblocked** when every ticket blocking it is closed; the **frontier** is the open, unblocked, unclaimed children — the edge of the known.

The answer isn't part of the body — it's recorded on resolution (see [Work through the map](#work-through-the-map)). Assets created while resolving a ticket are linked from the issue, not pasted in.

## Ticket Types

Every ticket is either **HITL** — human in the loop, worked *with* a human who speaks for themselves — or **AFK**, driven by the agent alone. A HITL ticket only resolves through that live exchange; the agent never stands in for the human's side of it (a grilling agent that answers its own questions has broken this).

- **Research** (AFK): Reading documentation, third-party APIs, or local resources like knowledge bases to surface a fact a decision waits on. Resolved by a `/research` **subagent**. Use when knowledge outside the current working directory is required.
- **Prototype** (HITL): Raise the fidelity of the discussion by making a cheap, rough, concrete artifact to react to — an outline, a rough take, a stub, or UI/logic code via the /prototype skill. Links the prototype as an asset. Use when "how should it look" or "how should it behave" is the key question.
- **Grilling** (HITL): Conversation via the /grilling and /domain-modeling skills, one question at a time. The default case.
- **Task** (HITL or AFK): Manual work that must happen before a *decision* can be made — nothing to decide, prototype, or research, but the discussion is blocked until it's done. Signing up for a service so its API can be judged, provisioning access, moving data so its shape can be seen. This is the one type that *does* rather than decides — and it earns its place by unblocking a decision, not by delivering the destination. The agent drives it alone where it can (AFK); otherwise it hands the human a precise checklist (HITL). Resolved when the work is done; the answer records what was done and any resulting facts (credentials location, new URLs, row counts) later tickets depend on.

## Fog of war

The map is _deliberately_ incomplete: don't chart what you can't yet see. Beyond the live tickets lies the **fog of war** — the dim view of decisions and investigations you can tell are coming but can't yet pin down, because they hang on questions still open. Resolving a ticket clears the fog ahead of it, graduating whatever's now specifiable into fresh tickets — one at a time, until the way to the destination is clear and no tickets remain.

The map's **Not yet specified** section is where that dim view is written down: the suspected question, the area to revisit later. It's the undiscovered frontier _toward_ the destination — everything here is in scope, just not sharp enough to ticket. Write as loosely or as fully as the view allows; it doubles as a signpost for collaborators reading where the effort is headed.

**Fog or ticket?** The test is whether you can state the question precisely now — _not_ whether you can answer it now.

- **Ticket when** the question is already sharp — even if it's blocked and you can't act on it yet.
- **Not yet specified when** you can't yet phrase it that sharply. Don't pre-slice the fog into ticket-sized pieces: it's coarser than a ticket, and one patch may graduate into several tickets, or none, once the frontier reaches it.

**Not yet specified** excludes what's already decided (Decisions so far), what's already a live ticket, and what's out of scope (the next section).

## Out of scope

Fog only ever gathers _toward_ the destination. The destination fixes the scope, so work beyond it is **out of scope** — it isn't fog, and it doesn't belong in **Not yet specified**. It gets its own **Out of scope** section on the map: work you've consciously ruled out of _this_ effort. Scope, not sharpness, lands it here.

Out-of-scope work never graduates — the frontier stops at the destination — so it returns only if the destination is redrawn, and then as a fresh effort, not a resumption.

Ruling something out of scope is a scoping act, not a step on the route. When a ticket that already exists turns out to sit past the destination — mis-scoped in while charting, or exposed by a resolution — **close it** (a closed ticket is unambiguously off the frontier) and leave one line in the **Out of scope** section: the gist plus why it's out of scope, linking the closed ticket. It stays out of **Decisions so far**, which records the route actually walked — a scope boundary isn't a step on it.

## Invocation

Two modes. Either way, **never resolve more than one ticket per session** — with the exception of research tickets.

### Chart the map

User invokes with a loose idea.

1. **Name the destination.** Run a `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling` session to pin down what this map is finding its way to — the spec, decision, or change. The destination fixes the scope, so it's settled first.
2. **Map the frontier.** Grill again, **breadth-first** this time: fan out across the whole space rather than deep on any one thread, surfacing the open decisions and the first steps takeable now. **If this surfaces no fog** — the way to the destination is already clear, the whole journey small enough for one session — you don't need a map. Stop and ask the user how they'd like to proceed.
3. **Create the map** (label `wayfinder:map`): Destination and Notes filled in, Decisions-so-far empty, the fog sketched into **Not yet specified**.
4. **Create the tickets you can specify now** as child issues of the map — then wire blocking edges in a **second pass** (issues need ids before they can reference each other). Wiring sorts them into the frontier and the blocked; everything you can't yet specify stays in the fog — the **Not yet specified** section.
5. **Fire the research subagents.** For each `research` ticket you just created, spin up a `/research` subagent to resolve it in parallel, capturing its findings on a throwaway `research/<name>` branch with a context pointer from the ticket.
6. Stop — charting is one session's work; it hand-resolves nothing.

### Work through the map

User invokes with a map (URL or number). A ticket is **optional** — without one, you pick the next decision, not the user.

1. Load the **map** — the low-res view, not every ticket body.
2. Choose the ticket. If the user named one, use it. Otherwise take the first frontier ticket in order. **Claim it**: assign it to yourself before any work.
3. Resolve it — **zoom as needed**: fetch the full body of any related or closed ticket on demand; invoke the skills the `## Notes` block names. If in doubt, use `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling`.
4. Record the resolution: post the answer as a **resolution comment**, **close** the issue, and **append a context pointer** to the map's Decisions-so-far.
5. Add newly-surfaced tickets (create-then-wire); graduate any fog the answer has made specifiable, clearing each graduated patch from **Not yet specified** so it lives only as its new ticket. If the answer reveals a ticket — this one or another — sits beyond the destination, **rule it out of scope** rather than resolving it on the route. If the decision invalidates other parts of the map, update or delete those tickets.

The user may run unblocked tickets in parallel, so expect other sessions to be editing the tracker concurrently.

skills.name: grilling
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/myankelev/.claude/skills/grilling

Interview me relentlessly about every aspect of this until we reach a shared understanding. Walk down each branch of the decision tree, resolving dependencies between decisions one-by-one. For each question, provide your recommended answer.

Ask the questions one at a time, waiting for feedback on each question before continuing. Asking multiple questions at once is bewildering.

If a *fact* can be found by exploring the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), look it up rather than asking me. The *decisions*, though, are mine — put each one to me and wait for my answer.

Do not act on it until I confirm we have reached a shared understanding.


ARGUMENTS: Resolve wayfinder ticket #814: where does the upload boundary sit relative to the durable op journal?

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- crypto-privacy-reviewer: Cryptography and privacy expert that reviews code, validates assumptions, and generates test cases. NOT prefixed with gsd- so it survives GSD updates. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash, Write)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

content.content:
{"body":"## Destination

A settled design and a dependency-linked chain of build slices covering the engine's **write plane** end to end: from a user mutation entering `Engine::command` to a record published, registered, and readable by the resolve/read path landed in #811. Content bytes are one layer of that plane, not the whole of it.

The map is done when nothing is left to decide — the slices can be filed against #655 and built.

## Notes

**Domain:** `crates/engine` (write plane, content plane, sync/op-queue, net/publish), `crates/core` (content-seal primitive, envelope/read-body encode), the engine's hand-written API client, and the API's upload/registry/quota surface.

**Skills every session should consult:** `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling` by default; `/research` for the AFK research tickets; `/codebase-design` and `/design-an-interface` for the shared publish port.

**Standing preferences for this effort:**

- `CONTEXT.md` is the ubiquitous language — use its terms exactly (op queue, pending-op overlay, dead-letter, register-first, name inventory, advisory pin row, content key, adoption gate, floor law, eager set).
- `blueprint/core.md` and `blueprint/engine.md` are normative; where they name an "open edge" or "judgment", that is an unmade decision this map owns.
- AGENTS.md rule 8 (encode/decode fail-closed symmetry, release-active `Err`, never `debug_assert!`) and rule 7 (zeroize at the terminal owner only) bind every decision here.
- Determinism is injected — entropy, time, and policy enter as seam traits; never a direct clock or RNG.
- This is a **planning** map. It produces decisions and a slice chain, not the implementation.

**Scoping calls already made (2026-07-27):**

- Chunk size, DAG fan-out shape, and retention defaults are **in scope** — this effort freezes them, with an engine-side KAT vector for the DAG root block.
- The pin-provider layer ships **all three** `PinMode`s (Hosted, External, Dual), with the #705 advisory-quota fix folded in.
- The publish driver is **one shared port**, later backing rotation's `WriteWavePublisher` / `ScopeRootPublisher` (#635) — not a second register-first implementation.

## Why this map exists

Reconnaissance (2026-07-27) established that the gap is not content-specific. The engine has **no production write plane at all**:

- `sync::rebase::replay` (`crates/engine/src/sync/rebase.rs:138`) has no `src/` caller.
- `sync/tick.rs::run_tick_loop` (`crates/engine/src/sync/tick.rs:178`) has no `src/` caller.
- `seal_read_body` / `encode_envelope` appear in the engine only inside `#[cfg(test)]` modules.
- `ApiClient::upload` and `ApiClient::quota` (`crates/engine/src/api/client.rs:292`, `:283`) have zero production callers.
- The content plane's write half — `seal_content` (`content/mod.rs:86`), `frame_and_seal` (`content/chunk.rs:78`), `dag::assemble` (`content/dag.rs:106`) — is built and KAT-frozen in core, and entirely orphaned.

Consequence: today a plain `mkdir` stages an op, emits `SnapshotUpdated`, and publishes nothing — the op sits in the queue forever. `Create { content: None }` is not implemented either; it fails silently rather than returning `Unimplemented`.

## Decisions so far

<!-- one line per closed ticket -->

- [where does the upload boundary sit relative to the durable op journal?](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/814) — seal at command time, stage the sealed bytes, upload at drain. Ratified rather than chosen: `sync/staging.rs:40-42` and `sync/op.rs:11-13` already bind it, and the staging budget only has meaning if upload is deferred. Surfaced #828 (staged-blob shape) and the missing `EngineError::OverBudget` surface.
- [how do the API's two pin-row ingress paths interact, and which byte total is authoritative?](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/826) — all three orderings are safe (shared per-CID advisory lock + `uq_pinned_cids_account_cid`); `sumHostedBytes` and `sumPinnedBytes` are equal today so the divergence is latent, not live; #705 confirmed (`advisory` is `users.byo` verbatim, tracking neither sum); and the orphan residual does **not** cover the upload-then-publish-fails rollback — the schema records no CID→name edge, so no server-side sweep is expressible without a schema change. Note: `.planning/research/pin-row-ingress.md` on branch `research/pin-row-ingress`.
- [what is the memory model for a content write, and the resulting max file size?](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/815) — the client slices the `File` and feeds chunks; the engine seals and stages each, owning framing policy; the op is journaled once at commit (stage-then-commit). Peak wasm heap O(chunk). **Max file size = the staging budget** (1 GiB placeholder), not the DAG ceiling (107.79 GiB) or the API's per-block 100 MiB. Forces #828 to per-block staging keys, splits `stage_op`, and puts stateful write handles in the facade. Surfaced #829.
- [what should chunk size, DAG fan-out shape, and retention defaults be?](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/816) — research: **fan-out is not forward-compatible with `decode_root`** (hard rejects at `dag.rs:183-187` and `:188-192`, plus a flat assumption in `leaf_range_for_byte_range`), so shipping flat is a real wire-format commitment; it fails closed and loud, never silently. 2 MiB chunks are unavailable (seal to 2 MiB + 40 B, over the trustless-gateway ceiling) — 1 MiB is the largest safe size, 256 KiB has no published rationale. Fresh per-version content keys mean **zero cross-version leaf dedup by construction**, so keep-all retention costs k × filesize. Note: `.planning/research/content-format-freeze.md` on branch `research/content-format-freeze` (commit `f9086a6ec`).

## Not yet specified

- **Optimistic overlay projection for content** — a pending upload renders with no size and no mtime (`sync/overlay.rs:48-52` bumps `content_version` only). What the UI shows between command and publish depends on where the upload boundary lands.
- **Upload-side op progress and `OpId` exposure** — `OpPhase` has only `Download*` variants (`facade.rs:438-445`) and `emit_op_progress` hardcodes `op_id: None` (`facade.rs:1524`). #807 needs per-file progress keyed on the upload's op id; the shape follows the drain driver.
- **Dead-letter population from replay** — `dead_letters` is filled only from the cold-start undecodable sweep (`facade.rs:1016`); `ReplayReport::dead_letters` never reaches it. Becomes specifiable once the drain driver exists.
- **Version retention and prune** — the blueprint's "keep all versions within quota, with an explicit user-initiated prune op" needs a concrete op and policy. `content/retention.rs` has `plan_prune` with no caller.
- **Interaction with #797 (`content_cids` threading into held records) and #786 (`undo_dest_add_versioned` into the seq-CAS publish envelope)** — both plug into the publish path this map designs; whether they are subsumed or stay separate depends on the shared publish port's shape.

## Out of scope

- **Streaming media and ranged reads** — `leaf_range_for_byte_range` (`content/read.rs:282`) stays uncalled by this effort; #641 owns the Service Worker byte pipe. The DAG shape decision here must not foreclose it.
- **The web UI wiring** — #807 consumes this plane; it is not part of designing it.
- **Engine mailbox route mismatch** — the engine client calls `/mailbox`, `/mailbox/{id}` (`api/client.rs:327,338,359`) while the API serves `/mailbox/messages` (`apps/api/src/mailbox/mailbox.controller.ts:30,58`). A real 404-on-first-use defect with no contract-test coverage at all, found during recon — unrelated to the write plane, filed as #827.

{"body":"## Destination

A settled design and a dependency-linked chain of build slices covering the engine's **write plane** end to end: from a user mutation entering `Engine::command` to a record published, registered, and readable by the resolve/read path landed in #811. Content bytes are one layer of that plane, not the whole of it.

The map is done when nothing is left to decide — the slices can be filed against #655 and built.

## Notes

**Domain:** `crates/engine` (write plane, content plane, sync/op-queue, net/publish), `crates/core` (content-seal primitive, envelope/read-body encode), the engine's hand-written API client, and the API's upload/registry/quota surface.

**Skills every session should consult:** `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling` by default; `/research` for the AFK research tickets; `/codebase-design` and `/design-an-interface` for the shared publish port.

**Standing preferences for this effort:**

- `CONTEXT.md` is the ubiquitous language — use its terms exactly (op queue, pending-op overlay, dead-letter, register-first, name inventory, advisory pin row, content key, adoption gate, floor law, eager set).
- `blueprint/core.md` and `blueprint/engine.md` are normative; where they name an "open edge" or "judgment", that is an unmade decision this map owns.
- AGENTS.md rule 8 (encode/decode fail-closed symmetry, release-active `Err`, never `debug_assert!`) and rule 7 (zeroize at the terminal owner only) bind every decision here.
- Determinism is injected — entropy, time, and policy enter as seam traits; never a direct clock or RNG.
- This is a **planning** map. It produces decisions and a slice chain, not the implementation.

**Scoping calls already made (2026-07-27):**

- Chunk size, DAG fan-out shape, and retention defaults are **in scope** — this effort freezes them, with an engine-side KAT vector for the DAG root block.
- The pin-provider layer ships **all three** `PinMode`s (Hosted, External, Dual), with the #705 advisory-quota fix folded in.
- The publish driver is **one shared port**, later backing rotation's `WriteWavePublisher` / `ScopeRootPublisher` (#635) — not a second register-first implementation.

## Why this map exists

Reconnaissance (2026-07-27) established that the gap is not content-specific. The engine has **no production write plane at all**:

- `sync::rebase::replay` (`crates/engine/src/sync/rebase.rs:138`) has no `src/` caller.
- `sync/tick.rs::run_tick_loop` (`crates/engine/src/sync/tick.rs:178`) has no `src/` caller.
- `seal_read_body` / `encode_envelope` appear in the engine only inside `#[cfg(test)]` modules.
- `ApiClient::upload` and `ApiClient::quota` (`crates/engine/src/api/client.rs:292`, `:283`) have zero production callers.
- The content plane's write half — `seal_content` (`content/mod.rs:86`), `frame_and_seal` (`content/chunk.rs:78`), `dag::assemble` (`content/dag.rs:106`) — is built and KAT-frozen in core, and entirely orphaned.

Consequence: today a plain `mkdir` stages an op, emits `SnapshotUpdated`, and publishes nothing — the op sits in the queue forever. `Create { content: None }` is not implemented either; it fails silently rather than returning `Unimplemented`.

## Decisions so far

<!-- one line per closed ticket -->

- [where does the upload boundary sit relative to the durable op journal?](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/814) — seal at command time, stage the sealed bytes, upload at drain. Ratified rather than chosen: `sync/staging.rs:40-42` and `sync/op.rs:11-13` already bind it, and the staging budget only has meaning if upload is deferred. Surfaced #828 (staged-blob shape) and the missing `EngineError::OverBudget` surface.
- [how do the API's two pin-row ingress paths interact, and which byte total is authoritative?](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/826) — all three orderings are safe (shared per-CID advisory lock + `uq_pinned_cids_account_cid`); `sumHostedBytes` and `sumPinnedBytes` are equal today so the divergence is latent, not live; #705 confirmed (`advisory` is `users.byo` verbatim, tracking neither sum); and the orphan residual does **not** cover the upload-then-publish-fails rollback — the schema records no CID→name edge, so no server-side sweep is expressible without a schema change. Note: `.planning/research/pin-row-ingress.md` on branch `research/pin-row-ingress`.
- [what is the memory model for a content write, and the resulting max file size?](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/815) — the client slices the `File` and feeds chunks; the engine seals and stages each, owning framing policy; the op is journaled once at commit (stage-then-commit). Peak wasm heap O(chunk). **Max file size = the staging budget** (1 GiB placeholder), not the DAG ceiling (107.79 GiB) or the API's per-block 100 MiB. Forces #828 to per-block staging keys, splits `stage_op`, and puts stateful write handles in the facade. Surfaced #829.
- [what should chunk size, DAG fan-out shape, and retention defaults be?](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/816) — research: **fan-out is not forward-compatible with `decode_root`** (hard rejects at `dag.rs:183-187` and `:188-192`, plus a flat assumption in `leaf_range_for_byte_range`), so shipping flat is a real wire-format commitment; it fails closed and loud, never silently. 2 MiB chunks are unavailable (seal to 2 MiB + 40 B, over the trustless-gateway ceiling) — 1 MiB is the largest safe size, 256 KiB has no published rationale. Fresh per-version content keys mean **zero cross-version leaf dedup by construction**, so keep-all retention costs k × filesize. Note: `.planning/research/content-format-freeze.md` on branch `research/content-format-freeze` (commit `f9086a6ec`).

## Not yet specified

- **Optimistic overlay projection for content** — a pending upload renders with no size and no mtime (`sync/overlay.rs:48-52` bumps `content_version` only). What the UI shows between command and publish depends on where the upload boundary lands.
- **Upload-side op progress and `OpId` exposure** — `OpPhase` has only `Download*` variants (`facade.rs:438-445`) and `emit_op_progress` hardcodes `op_id: None` (`facade.rs:1524`). #807 needs per-file progress keyed on the upload's op id; the shape follows the drain driver.
- **Dead-letter population from replay** — `dead_letters` is filled only from the cold-start undecodable sweep (`facade.rs:1016`); `ReplayReport::dead_letters` never reaches it. Becomes specifiable once the drain driver exists.
- **Version retention and prune** — the blueprint's "keep all versions within quota, with an explicit user-initiated prune op" needs a concrete op and policy. `content/retention.rs` has `plan_prune` with no caller.
- **Interaction with #797 (`content_cids` threading into held records) and #786 (`undo_dest_add_versioned` into the seq-CAS publish envelope)** — both plug into the publish path this map designs; whether they are subsumed or stay separate depends on the shared publish port's shape.

## Out of scope

- **Streaming media and ranged reads** — `leaf_range_for_byte_range` (`content/read.rs:282`) stays uncalled by this effort; #641 owns the Service Worker byte pipe. The DAG shape decision here must not foreclose it.
- **The web UI wiring** — #807 consumes this plane; it is not part of designing it.
- **Engine mailbox route mismatch** — the engine client calls `/mailbox`, `/mailbox/{id}` (`api/client.rs:327,338,359`) while the API serves `/mailbox/messages` (`apps/api/src/mailbox/mailbox.controller.ts:30,58`). A real 404-on-first-use defect with no contract-test coverage at all, found during recon — unrelated to the write plane, filed as #827.

content.content:
Part of #813

## Question

After a successful publish, does the write path seed the base snapshot and cache, or does the user eat a full resolve plus gateway round trip for bytes the device just held?

## Why it is a fork

`read_content` reads from the **base snapshot only** and returns `ContentUnavailable("content not yet published")` for any node with a pending op targeting it (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:1413-1427`). The realistic sequence is: user uploads a file, then immediately previews it. Unless publish success repaints the base snapshot, that preview either fails or takes a full `resolve` plus per-leaf gateway fetch for content that was in memory moments earlier.

## Candidates

1. **Publish success repaints the base snapshot**, mirroring what `project_child_version` already does for a read (`facade.rs:1386-1388`, `sync/project.rs:50-63`). The read then goes over the network but at least resolves.
2. **Additionally cache locally** — plaintext or sealed blocks. Note this reintroduces content at rest, which `sync/staging.rs:40-42` deliberately forbids for the staging store; if the answer is "cache sealed blocks", say where and under what budget.
3. **Do nothing** and accept the latency, on the grounds that the resolve is correct and the cost is a one-time round trip.

## What resolving looks like

Pick a candidate and state the invariant it establishes about what a client may believe about its own just-published write without re-resolving. Note that the adoption gate (AGENTS.md rule 6) applies to every resolved record — any local seeding must not become a way to skip it.

content.text:
Claiming [read-after-write](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/817). Before the first question, four facts from the code that reshape the ticket's framing:

**Repaint isn't optional for `Create`.** The overlay renders a pending create by upserting the node into a cloned view (`sync/overlay.rs:28-33`); the base is untouched. When the op dequeues after publish, the overlay drops it — so if publish doesn't repaint the base, the file the user just uploaded **disappears from the UI**. The ticket's candidate 3 ("do nothing") is unavailable for creates; it's only arguable for `UpdateContent`, where the node survives and merely shows a stale size.

**A stale read is reachable, not just a slow one.** `read_content_inner` falls back to `last_known_good` on `ResolveOutcome::NoUpdate` (`facade.rs:1483-1489`). IPNS propagation is not instant, so "upload then preview" can hit the cache and serve the **previous version** with no error — worse than the latency the ticket worries about.

**Our own records never enter the snapshot cache.** `resolve_gated` writes the cache only on `Adopted` (`net/resolve.rs:190`). If publish raises the sequence floor — which the floor law requires, else our own seq-5 publish leaves seq-4 replayable — then re-fetching our own record lands on `SequenceNotNewer { sequence == floor }` → `Current`, which does **not** cache (`resolve.rs:200-217`). So for every name we own, the last-known-good cache stays cold or stale forever unless the write path seeds it.

**Content blocks are self-verifying.** `read_block` checks `verify_cid` before returning any body (`content/read.rs:224-226`). A local sealed-block cache therefore can't forge content — unlike records, where the adoption gate is the trust decision. Caching sealed blocks is not a gate bypass.

content.text:
Fair — I jumped into a sub-decision without laying out the flow. Here's the whole thing.

## The upload flow as designed so far

```
┌─ CLIENT (JS) ────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ user picks a File, client slices it into chunks   [#815 ✓]   │
└──────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
               │ beginWrite → pushChunk × N → commitWrite
┌─ ENGINE, at command time ────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. seal each chunk with a fresh per-version ContentKey        │
│ 2. stage each sealed block, one staging key per block  [#828] │
│ 3. journal ONE op into the durable queue               [#814] │
│ 4. emit SnapshotUpdated — overlay renders the file optimistically │
└──────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
               │  ... later, online: the DRAIN (doesn't exist yet)
┌─ ENGINE, at drain ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 5. upload N leaf blocks + 1 DAG root to the API               │
│ 6. author the file's read-body { versions: [ {cid,size,…} ] } │
│ 7. seal it, sign an IPNS record, register + publish     [#819]│
│ 8. link the child ref into the parent folder, publish parent  │
│ 9. dequeue the op, free the staged bytes                      │
└──────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
               │
        ★ #817 DECIDES HERE ★  — publish succeeded. What does the device keep?
               │
┌─ LATER: the user clicks the file to preview it ──────────────┐
│ a. look up the node in the BASE snapshot  (overlay not consulted) │
│ b. resolve the file's own IPNS name over the network           │
│ c. fetch every leaf block from the gateway, unseal, concatenate│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Step 9 is the hinge. The moment the op dequeues, the overlay stops rendering it — the optimistic view is gone and only the base snapshot is left. Meanwhile the device is *sitting on* everything the reader in step (a)–(c) is about to go fetch: the read-body it authored, the record it signed, and the sealed blocks still in staging.

## What breaks, layer by layer

**Seed nothing.** The `Create` case is broken outright: at step 9 the overlay drops the file and the base snapshot never had it, so **the file the user just uploaded vanishes from the UI** until something re-resolves the parent folder. Then preview: step (b) resolves the file's name, but IPNS propagation isn't instant, so it can return `NoUpdate`; the fallback is the last-known-good cache, which for a name we own is **cold** — `resolve_gated` only caches records that pass the adoption gate (`net/resolve.rs:190`), and our own record can't (see below). Result: `ContentUnavailable: "no record source reachable and no cached record"`. When propagation *has* landed, it works, but step (c) re-downloads from a gateway every byte the device uploaded ninety seconds earlier.

**Seed the base snapshot.** Project the authored read-body into the base at step 9. The file stays visible — this one isn't really optional, it's the cost of having an overlay at all. Preview is unchanged: still a full resolve, still `NoUpdate`-fragile, still N gateway fetches.

**Also seed the record cache.** Write our own signed record bytes to `snapshot_cache` under the file's IPNS name. Now a `NoUpdate` on step (b) falls back to *our own current record* instead of nothing, so preview works during the propagation window, and survives a browser restart. The catch is a contract change: that seam's doc says "only gate-passing records ever reach this cache" (`seams/snapshot_cache.rs:14-16`), and this would be the first writer that isn't the gate.

This layer also fixes a bug that exists independently of read-after-write. The floor law requires publish to raise the sequence floor — otherwise we publish seq 5 and an attacker can still replay seq 4 past a floor sitting at 3. But once the floor is at 5, re-fetching our own record hits `SequenceNotNewer { sequence == floor }` → `ResolveOutcome::Current`, which doesn't write the cache (`resolve.rs:200-217`). So **for every name we own, the last-known-good cache is permanently cold unless the write path seeds it.** Offline cold-start renders nothing for your own files.

**Also cache the sealed blocks.** Preview becomes fully local, zero network. Safe on trust grounds — `read_block` verifies every body against its expected CID before returning it (`content/read.rs:224-226`), so a poisoned cache entry fails closed rather than forging content. Safe on the no-plaintext-at-rest rule too, since the blocks stay sealed. But it needs its own storage budget and eviction policy, and it can't just be "don't delete the staged bytes" — staging is budgeted as the write buffer (it's what caps max file size at ~1 GiB, per #815), so pinning read caches in there would starve future uploads. That means a distinct cache with a distinct budget, which is arguably a ticket of its own rather than a line in this one.

Each layer strictly contains the previous, and the useful question is where the line falls.

**Git hygiene — deviation, deliberate.** `git status` showed the shared checkout on a **sibling agent's branch** `research/content-format-freeze` (clean, tip `f9086a6ec`), not `main`. Running `git checkout -b … main` would have yanked the shared working tree out from under that agent — exactly the clobber the brief warned about. I created the branch via an isolated `git worktree` off `main` instead, committed there, then removed the worktree. Net result is identical (branch exists, one commit on a main commit) and the shared checkout is still on `research/content-format-freeze`, clean. Verified: `git show --stat HEAD` = 1 file, `git log --oneline -2` = my commit on `b91633b35`.

**Ten-line summary:**

1. `estimate()` cannot size the budget — the Storage Standard forbids quota being a function of free space, and Chrome "will always report 60% of the actual disk size"; `usage` is padded. A runtime fraction is confidently wrong.
2. Current per-origin quota: Chromium 60% total disk; Firefox min(10% disk, **10 GiB per-site group limit**); Safari 17+ ~60%; Safari <17 1 GiB. web.dev's Firefox/Safari numbers are years stale — MDN (2026-01-05) is the only accurate source.
3. Two Chromium modes bite below 1 GiB: incognito is a fraction of **RAM** (~400–550 MB on 8 GB), "clear on close" is a hard 300 MB.
4. **Staged bytes can be evicted, spec-mandated all-or-nothing per bucket.** IDB op queue + OPFS staged bytes die together — so no split-brain, but the whole offline divergence vanishes silently.
5. **Safari's ITP 7-day cap is the binding durability risk**, not quota: 7 days of browser use without a tap deletes everything. `persist()` exempts it — and we never call `persist()` anywhere.
6. `persist()` changes mode not quota, except Firefox where it's a 5× increase (and is user-prompted); Chrome/Safari auto-decide, WebKit essentially only for Home Screen apps.
7. **One shared constant is not defensible**: on desktop the budget is the FUSE `ENOSPC` threshold (`blueprint/desktop.md:184-186`), so 1 GiB means "no space left" on a 2 GiB file with 500 GB free.
8. **Live defect**: `stagingStore.ts:91` discards `SyncAccessHandle.write()`'s return — per spec a partial write returns `bytesWritten` rather than throwing, so a short write silently stages a truncated block that drain uploads under a mismatched CID. Same at `:114` for `read()`. AGENTS.md rule 8 shaped.
9. **Per-op reservation needed** — `stage_op` is read-then-write, so two concurrent `beginWrite`s both pass one budget check; needs an in-memory (non-durable) reservation ledger.
10. **Recommended (not decided)**: split into `staging_budget_bytes` (web 1 GiB / desktop 16 GiB floored by free space) and a new `max_file_bytes` (web 512 MiB / desktop 8 GiB); UI quotes the fixed constant, never `budget - staged`. Higher-leverage than the number: fix the ignored write/read returns, call `persist()`, add the ledger, map `QuotaExceededError` into #814's `EngineError::OverBudget`.</result>

content.text:
One gate. **The adoption gate** — six ordered stages (`gate/adoption.rs:43-56`), the only trust decision in the read path:

| | Stage | What it checks | Our own record |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `record-verify` | core's IPNS record verify chain | passes |
| 2 | `commitment-verify` | owner-signed grant-set commitment | passes |
| 3 | `grant-section` | seed-bearing structure sigs under committed pseudonyms | passes |
| 4 | `sequence` | strictly newer than the durable per-name floor | **the only one at risk** |
| 5 | `epoch` | envelope epoch ≥ scope read-epoch floor | passes |
| 6 | `unseal` | HPKE seed source + symmetric read-body unseal | passes |

So "gate-passing records" means records that cleared all six. My earlier framing was sloppy — I implied our own record is structurally ineligible. It isn't. Five stages pass trivially because we authored the bytes; only stage 4 is in question, and only because of *ordering*: if publish raises the sequence floor first, our record arrives at `sequence == floor`, which isn't strictly newer, so it's rejected as `SequenceNotNewer` and routed to `ResolveOutcome::Current` — the branch that doesn't cache.

That ordering turns out to be avoidable, and it changes the shape of this decision. `gate/floor.rs:6-13` says floors advance **only** on AAD-confirmed unseal — stage 6 — and that module is "the *only* place that advances them". So the write path shouldn't be raising the floor as a separate step at all. If publish instead feeds its own signed record bytes straight into the existing adopt path (no network fetch — we already hold the bytes), the record arrives with `sequence > floor`, passes stage 4, unseals at stage 6, and the floor raise, the cache write, and the projection all happen as ordinary consequences of the path that already exists.

Which means the seam contract change may be **zero**: the cache still only ever receives gate-passing records, because ours genuinely passed. It also gives rule 8 for free — we decode and verify our own encoded record before trusting it, so an encoder bug surfaces at publish instead of shipping bytes our own reader rejects.

On the sealed-block cache: agreed, and I'll record it as out of this decision's scope with its own ticket, since it needs a budget and eviction policy that don't exist yet.

content.text:
Focused on complexity and invalidation, then.

First, a correction to the example I gave for why publish must touch the floor — my numbers were wrong, though the conclusion holds. The real shape: our floor sits at 3, another device published 4, we seq-CAS publish 5 without ever adopting 4. Floor is still 3. Someone now serves record 4 — a genuine, correctly-signed record — and the gate sees `4 > 3`, adopts it, overwrites the cache, and reprojects. **The file the user just wrote reverts to the previous version.** Not an attack, just an ordinary stale copy on some IPFS node, and it silently undoes the write. That's the case that forces a floor advance at publish.

This matters for the option comparison, because it means "base snapshot only" doesn't escape the floor question. It still has to advance the floor, so it inherits the same invariant problem as the direct-write option — and it needs a hand-written projector besides.

## Complexity

| | Through the gate | Direct writes | Base snapshot only |
|---|---|---|---|
| Verify our record | reuses `adopt()` | none | none |
| Advance the floor | free, stage 6 | new call site | still needed |
| Write the cache | free, `Adopted` arm | new call site | skipped |
| Project the base | reuses `project_root` | hand-written | hand-written |
| New code | one `adopt_local(name, bytes)` — the `Adopted` arm of `resolve_gated` minus the fetch, ~30 lines | 2 seam calls + a projector | 1 floor call + a projector |
| Docs to amend | none | `snapshot_cache.rs:14-16`, `gate/floor.rs:6-13` | `gate/floor.rs:6-13` |

The direct-writes option looks cheapest at the call site and isn't. `gate/floor.rs:6-13` states that module is "the *only* place that advances" floors, and `snapshot_cache.rs:14-16` states "only gate-passing records ever reach this cache." Both are load-bearing reasoning shortcuts: today you can look at a cached record and know it was verified, and look at a floor and know it moved only on AAD-confirmed unseal. A second writer to each costs you both properties permanently, to save one HPKE unseal per publish.

Going through the gate also buys the rule-8 property free — we decode and verify our own encoding before trusting it, so an encoder bug fires at publish rather than shipping records our own reader rejects.

## Cache invalidation

This is the part I'd stop worrying about. The record cache is a **single slot per IPNS name** — `cache_key = name.as_str().as_bytes()`, `put` replaces (`resolve.rs:176,190`). No TTL, no version list, no eviction. There is no invalidation policy to design; invalidation *is* the next successful adopt overwriting the slot.

Monotonicity is enforced by the floor rather than the cache, so a stale record can't overwrite a fresher one — it fails stage 4 before reaching the `put`. And going through the gate can't corrupt the cache with something the read path would reject, because it's literally the read path.

One genuinely new state, common to every option that seeds: publish reports success but the record never becomes resolvable network-side. Our cache then asserts a version other devices can't see. It self-heals on the next successful publish, and the content blocks are separately pinned so no bytes are lost — but it should be named as accepted, and the recovery belongs to [ordering and rollback](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/819).

The real invalidation complexity all lives in the sealed-block cache you want deferred — budget, eviction, survive-logout — which is exactly why it's separable.

content.text:
Recorded. Next fork, and it's the one that decides how much protection the self-adopt actually gives.

If the self-adopt runs *after* publish, a gate rejection tells you your encoder produced a record your own reader refuses — but by then the bad record is already on the network, signed and resolvable by every other device. The check has diagnostic value and no preventive value.

A non-advancing verify already exists for exactly this shape: `open_at_floor`, used by the `Current`/`NoUpdate` arms of the read path, where the comment notes "neither advances a floor" (`facade.rs:1476-1478`). So a pre-publish dry run is available off the shelf.

It has to be a *separate* run from the real adopt, not a reordering. Stage 6 advances the floor, and advancing it before a publish that then fails is actively harmful: if our publish dies and another device legitimately publishes at that same sequence, our floor now rejects their record as not-newer and we ignore a valid record indefinitely. So the floor advance must stay strictly downstream of publish success.

input.content:
## Resolution

**Publish self-adopts: the write path feeds its own signed record bytes back through the adoption gate, with a non-advancing dry run before the record ever leaves the device.**

```
author read-body → seal → sign record
  └─ verify_local(name, bytes)        no floor effect, no cache write
       reject → fail the op, publish NOTHING
  └─ publish (register-first, #819 owns the ordering)
       └─ adopt_local(name, bytes)    the Adopted arm of resolve_gated, minus the fetch
            ├─ stage 6 → advance_sequence_on_unseal()
            ├─ snapshot_cache.put(name, bytes)
            └─ project → base snapshot
```

### Why through the gate rather than direct writes

Not raising the floor at publish silently reverts the user's write, with no attacker required. Floor at 3; another device published 4; we seq-CAS publish 5 without ever adopting 4. A client may render and read its own just-published write without re-resolving, because the bytes it is trusting passed the same six-stage gate any remote record must pass. **It may skip the fetch; it never skips the gate.**

Part of #813

## Question

What does the pending-op overlay render for a content write between `commitWrite` and publish — and where do the size and mtime come from?

## Why it is now specifiable

Graduated from the map's fog. #814 settled that upload is deferred past the journal, #815 settled that the client feeds chunks and the op is journaled once at commit, and #817 settled what the base snapshot holds *after* publish. The remaining gap is the window in between, which is now the only unrendered stretch of a content write.

## The gap

`apply_overlay` bumps `content_version` and nothing else for an `UpdateContent` op (`sync/overlay.rs:48-52`), and a `Create` upserts a bare `NodeMeta::new(target, name, kind)` (`:28-33`) — no size, no mtime. So a file the user just uploaded renders with no size until publish repaints the base snapshot, which under #817 may be minutes later if the device is offline.

The engine knows the size: the client declares the total at `beginWrite` (#815), so it is in hand before the op is journaled. Whether it is *carried* on the op is the open part — `OpKind::UpdateContent` holds only `content_staging_key` today (`sync/op.rs`).

## What to establish

1. Whether the op carries a declared plaintext size and an authored mtime, or the overlay leaves both absent and the UI renders a pending state without them.
2. If carried: what the client is entitled to believe about a size that has not been published, given the overlay "renders intent" and never rebases (`sync/overlay.rs:5-10`). A declared size that the sealed content later contradicts is a caller-contract violation — decide whether it is checked at `commitWrite`, and fail-closed if so.
3. What mtime a pending write shows. Time is injected (determinism seam), so this is an authored value, not a clock read.
4. Whether `OpPhase` gains upload-side variants here or in the drain-driver slice — it has only `Download*` today (`facade.rs:438-445`) and `emit_op_progress` hardcodes `op_id: None` (`:1524`). #807 needs per-file progress keyed on the upload's op id. Coordinate with #824, which owns op identity at the facade.
5. Whether a queued-but-unpublished file is distinguishable in the rendered snapshot from a published one — the UI needs to show a pending badge, and today the overlay leaves no mark.

## Constraint

The overlay is deliberately not the rebase: it never drops, suffixes, or dead-letters (`sync/overlay.rs:5-10`). Whatever this ticket adds stays pure projection of intent over the gate-passing base.

Surfaced while resolving #817 (wayfinder map #813), and ruled out of that map's scope: it is a read-path optimization, not part of the write plane.

## What

A durable cache of **sealed** content blocks, so reading a file the device recently wrote or read does not refetch every leaf from a gateway.

## Why it is safe

- `read_block` verifies every body against its expected CID before returning it (`crates/engine/src/content/read.rs:224-226`), so a poisoned or corrupted cache entry fails closed rather than forging content. Unlike records, where the adoption gate is the trust decision, content blocks are self-verifying by address.
- Blocks stay sealed at rest, so the no-plaintext-at-rest rule that governs the staging store (`sync/staging.rs:40-42`) is preserved.

## Why it is not urgent

Read-after-write does not need it. The read source order is accelerator-first (`content/read.rs:86-88`), and the accelerator is the Kubo node the upload just pinned the blocks to — so freshly written blocks have no propagation window the way IPNS records do. This is latency, never correctness.

## What it needs

1. **Its own budget, separate from the staging budget.** Staging is the write buffer and is what caps maximum file size (#815, #829); pinning read caches inside it would starve uploads. Note #829's finding that a single shared constant is not defensible across web and desktop.
2. **An eviction policy** — the first cache in the engine that needs one. The record cache is a single slot per IPNS name, overwritten on adopt, with no eviction at all (`net/resolve.rs:176,190`); a block cache is many-entry and unbounded by nature.
3. **A decision on whether entries survive logout.** `SnapshotCache` contents survive by design, cleared only by an explicit "forget this device" (`seams/snapshot_cache.rs:15-17`). Whether sealed content blocks get the same treatment is a privacy call, not a copy of that default.
4. **A host-storage answer**, given #829: staged bytes are evictable, spec-mandated all-or-nothing per bucket, and Safari's ITP 7-day cap applies unless `persist()` is called — which we never call.
5. **A seam decision**: reuse `SnapshotCache` with content-CID keys, or introduce a distinct `BlockCache` seam. The existing seam's contract says only gate-passing *records* reach it, so reuse means widening a deliberately narrow contract.

## Not in scope here

Ranged reads and streaming media (#641) — `leaf_range_for_byte_range` (`content/read.rs:282`) stays uncalled. A block cache should not foreclose it, but does not deliver it either.

    "still awaits `resolve()`; the seed rescues the `NoUpdate` arm. Surfaced #830, ruled the "
    "sealed-block cache out of scope (#831).\n"
)

marker = "\n## Not yet specified"
assert body.count(marker) == 1
body = body.replace(marker, decision + marker)

fog = (

open("/tmp/newbody.md", "w").write(body)
subprocess.run(["env", "-u", "GITHUB_TOKEN", "gh", "api", "-X", "PATCH",
                "repos/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/813", "-F", "body=@/tmp/newbody.md",
                "--jq", ".number"], check=True)

content.text:
[Read-after-write](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/817) is resolved and closed, and the map is updated.

**The decision: publish self-adopts.** The write path feeds its own signed record bytes back through the adoption gate — no fetch — with a non-advancing `open_at_floor` dry run before the record leaves the device. The dry run means a bad encoding fails the op locally instead of signing and publishing bytes our own reader rejects; the post-publish adopt then produces the floor advance, the cache write, and the base-snapshot projection as ordinary consequences of a path that already exists.

The hinge was that the write path must **not** raise the sequence floor itself. Do that and our record arrives at `sequence == floor`, gets rejected as `SequenceNotNewer`, and routes to the one arm that doesn't cache. Leave the floor alone and all six stages pass, so both single-writer invariants survive untouched — *cached implies gate-passing*, *floors move only on unseal* — with no seam doc amended. The invariant recorded: a client may skip the fetch for its own write, never the gate.

Two things worth carrying forward. My earlier justification for the floor advance used wrong numbers; the real case is floor at 3, another device published 4, we CAS-publish 5 without adopting 4 — any node still serving record 4 satisfies `4 > 3`, so the gate adopts it and **the user's write silently reverts**. No attacker needed. And "do nothing" was never actually a candidate: the overlay renders a pending create into a cloned view, so at dequeue the file would vanish from the UI.

**Filed:** [what the overlay renders before publish](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/830) — graduated from the map's fog, now that both ends of the window are settled; wired to block the decomposition ticket. And [the sealed content-block read cache](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/831) as a v2-build issue, ruled **out of scope** for this map rather than deferred within it — it's read-path latency, and the accelerator-first source order means the node serving reads is the one the upload just pinned to, so it's never a correctness requirement. Blocked by the staging-budget ticket, since it needs a budget that isn't staging's.

**Frontier is now 6:** [content key custody](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/818), [ordering and rollback](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/819), [pin-provider layer](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/822), [cancel semantics](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/824), [staged blob shape](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/828), [overlay projection](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/830). Ordering-and-rollback picks up two constraints from this decision, so it's the natural next one.

On the parked research: the two defects it found are captured in the comment on [the staging budget ticket](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/829), so they're not at risk of being lost, but neither belongs to that ticket's question. The `stagingStore.ts:91` one is the sharper of the two — `SyncAccessHandle.write()` returns `bytesWritten` on a short write rather than throwing, so today a truncated block stages silently and drain uploads it under a CID that won't match. Want me to file those two as their own defect issues?

   - **The adoption gate** — the single trust decision in the read path, six ordered stages: `record-verify`, `commitment-verify`, `grant-section`, `sequence`, `epoch`, `unseal`.
   - **The floor law** — durable monotonic-max per-scope epoch floors and per-name sequence floors; advances only on AAD-confirmed unseal (stage 6), cold-seed from a re-point object, or pointer `writeEpoch` on sight; regression is fail-closed.
   - **Cache-first / last-known-good** — `SnapshotCache` seam holds ciphertext-only records, single slot per IPNS name, written only on gate pass.
   - **Pending-op overlay / state law** — rendered state = last-known-good snapshot ⊕ pending-op overlay; the overlay renders *intent*, never rebases.
   - **Stage-then-commit write protocol** (from #815) — `beginWrite` → `pushChunk × N` → `commitWrite`; one op journaled at commit; per-block staging keys (#828).
   - **AGENTS.md rule 8** — encode/decode fail-closed symmetry; a decode-side hard reject needs a matching **release-active** `Err` on the produce path, never `debug_assert!`/`assert!`.
   - **AGENTS.md rule 7** — zeroize at the terminal owner only; a callee must not zero caller-owned buffers.
   - **AGENTS.md rule 6** — every resolved record passes the adoption gate; a failure is a fail-closed trust violation, never mere staleness.
   - Determinism injected via seam traits — entropy, time, and policy enter as parameters; never a direct clock or RNG in core/engine logic.

3. **Files and Code Sections:**

   - **`crates/engine/src/gate/adoption.rs:43-160`** — the decisive file for the resolution. Defines the six-stage gate:
     ```rust
     pub enum GateStage {
         RecordVerify,      // Stage 1: core's IPNS record verify chain.
         CommitmentVerify,  // Stage 2: the owner-signed grant-set commitment.
         GrantSection,      // Stage 3: seed-bearing structure signatures under committed pseudonyms.
     ```
