===== 786 =====
786 OPEN engine: wire undo_dest_add_versioned into the seq-CAS publish envelope
From the #781 review (closes #743). `undo_dest_add_versioned` (fail-closed versioned compare-and-remove for dest-add compensation, keyed on the dest parent IPNS record sequence) ships as an unwired primitive — it has no non-test caller. When the publish/CAS wiring lands, the compensation call site MUST use the versioned variant, thread `observed` from the SAME dest-parent record read that the publish seq-CAS asserts against, and on `Conflict` re-read the dest parent at its new sequence and re-derive. Add an adversarial concurrent-writer interleave test at that seam. Part of #635


===== 797 =====
797 OPEN engine: re-pin content CIDs on sub-EOL renewal by threading content_cids into held records
Held records renew with empty `content_cids` (the resolve-tick loop in `facade.rs` builds `HeldMaterial` with `content_cids: Vec::new()`). The `head_cid` is now correctly derived from the adopted record (per the #789 HIGH fix), so the renewed record is **valid** — but no content is re-pinned on sub-EOL renewal, so content the accelerator holds can be GC'd over time even while the record stays alive.

**Acceptance:** thread the resolved root's content CIDs into the held record so `eol_renew_pass` re-registers/pins them on renewal, keeping content alive on the accelerator alongside the record. Add a renewal test asserting the republished registration carries the content CIDs.

Surfaced by the #789 crypto + security reviews as the deferred re-pin boundary. Part of #752.


===== 635 =====
635 OPEN engine: implement rotation primitives, sweep, name wave, and grants
## Scope

The three primitives with no recovery machinery: rotateScope (override seed mint, eager set law — owner cascade over every transitively-reachable descendant scope root fully rotated vs grantee flat self-contained, grant blobs re-wrapped verbatim for the committed set, owner blob, history link, ascent link, structure-signed by the rotator's writer pseudonym); sweep (idempotent epoch-lag work-list, epoch-converged pre-grant convergence, direct-child-scope index self-heal, metadata-only re-seal, idle-cadence Scheduler job, CAS-safe concurrent sweepers); rotateScopeWrite (commitment re-sign, write override seed, background child-first name wave with root re-pointed last, three-channel re-point publish, inventory swap via register-first and batch retire, root linger). The full trigger table including full-depth scope-exit detection, immediate-cut read revoke, write revoke/downgrade, discovered link expiry, manual rotate-now; grant creation (converge, mint scope at epoch 1, write-scope cut, parent index update, publish, mailbox share pointer) and invites (ephemeral-key blobs, bearer write-link flagging, claim conversion).
Does NOT land: scheduled hygiene rotation (designed-for, deferred).

## Blueprint anchors

`blueprint/engine.md`: Rotation primitives; Grants and ledger (grant creation, invites); Pointer planes (re-point publish)

## Gate

Engine simulation: the trigger table and eager-set law mirrored 1:1, sweep idempotence and concurrent sweepers, resumed name waves via the write-plane history link, crash-recovery from published records only, immediate cut, forgery-window bounds, grant-creation convergence requirement.

## Depends on

- #628 (engine: build the gated resolve and publish pipeline and liveness jobs)
- #632 (engine: implement the sync core with op queue, rebase, and pointers)
- #633 (engine: add the grants ledger, contact import, and mailbox logic)

content.text:
Claimed [design the one shared publish port](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/821) and read the ground. One part of the ticket's question 1 is already settled by evidence, so I'm not asking it: the port cannot **replace** `net::publish::publish`. Liveness's sub-EOL renewal (`net/liveness.rs:28`) and revival (`net/revival.rs:15`) both publish an already-known head CID and author nothing — revival recovers its CID from the endpoint (`net/revival.rs:22-24`), and the keyless re-PUT never publishes at all. Forcing those through an authoring layer they have no inputs for is strictly worse. So `publish` survives as the register/CAS/PUT mechanic and the port sits above it.

What's genuinely open is **how much** sits above it. Three ingredients are in play, and today none of them has a production caller: authoring (`seal_read_body`/`encode_envelope` appear in the engine only inside `#[cfg(test)]`), head-block upload (`ApiClient::upload`, `api/client.rs:292`), and #817's self-adopt.

**Option A — a thin "install this record" port.** Takes finished head-block bytes + name + signer + content CIDs; uploads the block, calls `publish`, returns the published record bytes.

- *For:* smallest new surface, and the existing rotation ports map onto it almost verbatim — `ScopeRootPublisher::publish_scope_root` (`rotation/rotate.rs:98-107`) and `WriteWavePublisher::republish` (`rotate_write.rs:167`) both already take an assembled-record struct. No key material and no reader context enter the port, so the zeroize surface stays where it is.
- *Against:* authoring is the part that doesn't exist and the part that must be identical across callers. Leaving it out doesn't prevent two register-first implementations — it relocates the duplication one layer up, into exactly the `#745`/`#746` wiring both rotation ports say is deferred ("assembling the record bytes … is the deferred #745/#746 wiring", `rotate_write.rs:120-123`). And #817's dry-run-then-adopt needs the envelope plus a `ReaderContext`, so self-adopt also lands outside the port, in every caller.

**Option B — an "author, publish, and adopt one node record" port.** Takes a node-level intent (node id, scope, epoch, read body, section disposition, signer, content CIDs, reader context) and runs seal → encode → CID → upload → publish → self-adopt.

- *For:* it is the whole missing production write path in one place, and the ordering that's actually easy to get wrong is internal. The rule-8 encode-side guards live at one boundary rather than per caller. `adopt_deferred` (`gate/adoption.rs:421`) already has exactly the shape #817 wants — hand-fed `Candidate`, floors advanced only on an explicit `commit` — so self-adopt needs no new plumbing, just a caller.
- *Against:* the read body means three different things across callers. A content write supplies a new body at the same epoch with the section carried verbatim; a read rotation re-seals at a new epoch under a new key (`rotate.rs:49-54`); the write wave carries the sealed read body verbatim and re-seals only the write body (`rotate_write.rs:120-123`). One parameter with three meanings tends to become a union with a branch per caller. It also pulls read-key material into the port.

**Option C — a pure `author_record` alongside a thin install port.** A is the port; authoring becomes three named pure functions; the drain composes author → install → adopt.

- *For:* the authoring modes get distinct names instead of a union parameter, and pure authoring is KAT-testable the way `crates/core` already is. Self-adopt composes at the drain, which is where the snapshot seeding belongs anyway.
- *Against:* the scoping call on the map was explicitly *one* shared port, and this ships two things. The sequencing discipline — author, upload head, register, publish, adopt, only then commit floors — is the correctness-critical part, and C hands it back to each caller to get right.

The evidence leans to **B**, on one fact: the thing that must not be duplicated isn't the PUT (that's already unduplicated inside `publish`) but the *ordering* around it, and A and C both leave that ordering to callers. The read-body-parameter objection to B is real but narrower than it looks — the three modes differ in what produces the sealed bytes, not in what happens to them afterwards, so B can take `Envelope` + section disposition rather than a raw read body, which pushes the three modes upstream without pushing the ordering out.

Here's the higher-level frame I should have led with. B and B′ look like a parameter-shape choice; they're actually a **custody** choice — does the port hold read-key material, or only signing material?

**The precedent that's at stake.** The layer directly below has an explicit, documented stance: `PublishRequest.signer` is "derived in the key-lifecycle slice; injected here so this slice owns no key derivation" (`net/publish.rs:41-43`). The whole net layer today is custody-free apart from an injected Ed25519 signer. B reverses that stance for the layer immediately above it; B′ extends it. In a codebase where every crypto-touching diff pulls a mandatory `/crypto-privacy-review`, that stance decides whether the write plane's busiest component is permanently on the crypto review path or permanently off it.

**What the port would actually be sealing.** I overstated the three-modes problem earlier. Checking `reseal_scope_root` (`rotation/reseal.rs:198`): it produces a signed `GrantSection` and stops — the read-body seal and envelope encode are deliberately left to "the publisher" (`rotation/rotate.rs:49-54`). And of the three callers, the write-plane name wave carries the sealed read body verbatim and seals nothing. So there is really **one** sealing shape — `(read_key, epoch, ReadBody) → Envelope` — used by the content write and the read rotation, plus a carry-verbatim case. B's union-parameter risk is smaller than I made it sound: it's a two-armed "seal this / carry these bytes", not three shapes.

**But B′'s custody advantage may be illusory, and this is the crux.** #817's self-adopt runs the gate, and the gate's `ReaderContext` borrows a `read_key` (`net/adopter.rs:158-166`). That is the *same* read key the seal would need. So if the port closes the #817 loop internally, it holds a read key whether or not it seals — and B′ buys nothing. B′ only genuinely stays custody-free if self-adopt *also* sits outside the port, at which point the port has shrunk most of the way back to A and the #817 requirement becomes "return the bytes so the drain can adopt them."

So B′ as I drafted it is an unstable midpoint. The honest spectrum is a single question about where the custody boundary falls:

**Custody-bearing port.** Owns node-state → adopted snapshot: seals, publishes, self-adopts, commits floors.
- *For:* the AAD binding (`v`/`id`/`scope`/`epoch`) is asserted in the same place the gate will re-derive it, instead of being assembled independently by two callers — an epoch mis-binding is a fail-closed gate rejection at best. The #817 dry-run can't be forgotten. Rotation's deferred #745/#746 envelope wiring lands here rather than being written twice.
- *Against:* breaks the net layer's no-key-derivation stance; every publish test needs full key setup rather than dummy bytes; permanently crypto-review-gated.

**Custody-free port.** Bytes → network → bytes back: takes an `Envelope` (or a finished head block), uploads, registers, CAS-publishes, returns the signed record bytes. Sealing and self-adopt both belong to the caller.
- *For:* extends the existing stance exactly; fakeable with arbitrary bytes; the crypto surface stays in `crates/core` and the adopter where it already lives.
- *Against:* the write plane's authoring function still has to exist somewhere and doesn't today, so this doesn't remove work — it relocates it. And the #817 ordering (dry-run before PUT, adopt after, floors last) becomes the drain's discipline to hold rather than a structural guarantee.

The two differ from option C only in whether that authoring function is named as its own deliverable with its own KAT vectors.

content.text:
Fair question, and the honest accounting is that the additions buy **less than they appear to**, plus one thing that's real.

**What they don't buy, on inspection:**

- *AAD binding assembled once.* This looked like the strongest argument and it isn't. #817 already mandates a non-advancing `open_at_floor` dry run before the record reaches the network, and a wrong `(v, id, scope, epoch)` binding fails that dry run wherever it lives. The dry run is the structural protection, not custody.
- *Rotation gets #745/#746 envelope wiring free.* Rotation has to unseal the read body to re-seal it at the new epoch anyway (that's what its cascade resolver is for), and it derives the new read key from the override seed it just minted. So the port would be handed a key rotation already computed, to make a call rotation could make itself. The saving is roughly four lines: `seal_read_body` → `encode_envelope` → `compute_cid`.
- *One place for rule-8 encode guards.* They're already elsewhere and staying there — `body.validate()` fires inside `seal_read_body` (`envelope.rs:131`), `assert_children_unique` is in core, and the empty-head-CID guard is already in `publish` (`publish.rs:133-135`).

**What they do buy:** a structural guarantee that nothing reaches the network un-dry-run. If the drain seals and the port publishes, nothing in the type system stops a caller from handing over an envelope it never preflighted.

**And there's a cost I hadn't surfaced that I think settles it against custody-bearing.** A custody-bearing port needs a read key on *every* publish — including liveness's sub-EOL renewal and revival, which have neither. `HeldRecord` deliberately stores only the narrow per-name Ed25519 signer, explicitly *not* the scope write seed, because holding the seed would derive the full write plane for every node in the scope (`net/liveness.rs:44-52` — "least privilege; security rules 2 and 5"). Custody-bearing would force read keys into the held set, against a documented least-privilege decision, or exclude those callers — at which point it isn't the one shared port the map scoped.

So your lean is right: **custody-free**. That leaves exactly one thing to recover — the dry-run guarantee — and it can be bought without custody.

content.text:
`fanout_get_verify` collapses three different situations into `None` (`net/fanout.rs:96-116`): every endpoint erroring, every endpoint serving no record, and every endpoint serving unverifiable garbage. It cannot tell "the network is unreadable" from "our record isn't there". So the port can't repair this by looking harder — it can only choose what to report.

One mechanical fact makes this cheaper than it looks: the sequence floor advances only when the gate unseals (stage 6), and under custody-free the port doesn't adopt. So a republish after an unconfirmed publish reads the *same* floor and mints the *same* sequence — a re-PUT of an equivalent record, not sequence churn. Retrying an unconfirmed publish costs one signature and one fan-out.

**Option 1 — keep reporting `Published` (status quo, `publish.rs:183-190`).**
- *For:* an ack from at least one endpoint is real evidence; a read-back miss is ordinary propagation lag through someguy and the public gateways, and this is the common case on a healthy network.
- *Against:* it is precisely the mechanism behind the residual #817 accepted. Under #819 the op is removed on publish success, so a record that acked but never became resolvable has no queue-based recovery — the self-heal is the *next* write at that name, which for a rarely-touched folder may be never.

**Option 2 — a third outcome, `Unconfirmed { sequence }`.**
- *For:* it preserves the distinction instead of destroying it, and hands the choice to #819's failure classification, where "availability → retry indefinitely" already lives. The drain can keep the op queued; liveness and revival can treat it as success and move on. Because the floor hasn't moved, the retry is idempotent-in-sequence.
- *Against:* a new variant every caller must handle, including the two rotation port adapters. And it converts a currently-silent condition into one the drain must have a policy for — head-of-line blocking under #819 means a persistently-unreadable endpoint set could stall the queue behind a write that actually landed.

**Option 3 — treat it as a failure (`PublishError`).**
- *For:* fail-closed matches the repo's doctrine, and the retry is cheap for the reason above.
- *Against:* it fails closed on the wrong axis. Unresolvability is an *availability* fact, not a trust violation — the gate's whole design separates those, and #819 already classifies availability failures as retry-forever. Reporting a durable-ack publish as an error also mis-signals to liveness's renewal path, which has no rebase to fall back on.

The evidence points at **Option 2**. Option 1 is the one the map already recorded as a known residual, and Option 3 conflates availability with trust in a codebase that keeps those strictly apart.

content.text:
Two more consequences are forced rather than open, so I'll state them instead of asking: **#797 stays a separate slice** (it fixes `HeldMaterial` in the resolve-tick loop, and liveness's renewal never goes through the new layer at all — it has a head CID, not a head block), and **content-block upload stays with the drain** (the port takes CIDs; rotation republishes existing content and uploads nothing). **#786 also stays separate, but its acceptance criterion needs amending** — it says to thread `observed` from "the SAME dest-parent record read that the publish seq-CAS asserts against", and no such read exists: the expectation comes from the durable floor (`publish.rs:149-154`), never from an observed record. I'll record that on the issue.

That leaves the shape question, and it turns out to be sharper than the ticket framed it. Under custody-free, the port's additions over `net::publish::publish` are exactly three: upload the head block, require the preflight witness, and return `Unconfirmed`. Everything else — register-first, floor+1, fan-out PUT, confirm — is already there. So the real question is whether this is a new layer at all.

**Option A — a thin new module above `publish`.** Takes the witness-wrapped head block, name, signer, content CIDs; uploads the block, calls `publish`, returns the signed record bytes plus outcome.
- *For:* `publish` stays exactly as it is for liveness and revival, which author nothing, have no block to upload, and have no envelope to preflight. The new module is where #817's ordering and #819's referent-before-reference sequencing live, and rotation's two trait impls call it — which is what the map's scoping call already described as "backing" them.
- *Against:* two functions with near-identical signatures sitting one on top of the other, and nothing stops a new caller from reaching past the wrapper straight to `publish`, bypassing the witness.

**Option B — extend `publish` itself.** Add an optional head block and the witness to `PublishRequest`; add `Unconfirmed` to the outcome.
- *For:* one function, one entry point, no bypass — the witness becomes universal.
- *Against:* the witness would need an "already-adopted bytes" constructor for liveness and revival, which is the bypass again with extra steps. And `PublishRequest` grows fields that are `None` for two of its three callers — the shape that reliably rots.

**Option C — make the port a Rust trait.**
- *For:* the drain and rotation's adapters both depend on an interface, testable without wiring seams.
- *Against:* the net layer is uniformly free functions over seam generics (`publish`, `revive`, `fanout_*`), and rotation's existing traits already exist to keep its *orchestration* pure — a second trait behind them adds an indirection whose only implementation is the concrete one.

The evidence points at **A**: the two callers that would force optional fields into `publish` are precisely the two that never author a record.

Measured it — it's disproportionate.

**Work.** `pub(crate)` would achieve nothing, because the callers we'd be guarding against (rotation, the future sync drain) are in the same crate. It has to be `pub(super)`, visible only inside `net/`. That's free for production — `publish` has exactly two non-test callers, `liveness.rs:201` and `revival.rs:84`, both already inside `net/`. The cost is entirely in tests: `crates/engine/tests/net.rs` is an external integration crate, 1160 lines, and calls `publish` at nine sites (368, 411, 447, 509, 553, 616, 661, 853, 1028). All nine break. Its fakes come from the public `testkit::fakes`, so the harness is portable, but you'd be relocating nine tests plus their local fixtures into a `#[cfg(test)]` module in `src/net/publish.rs` — and splitting what `blueprint/testing.md` treats as *the* net-plane simulation harness across two homes.

**Benefit.** Narrower than it first looks. The bug it guards against is publishing a record whose head block was never uploaded — nasty, because confirm-by-re-resolve still succeeds (the *record* resolves fine) and the failure only shows up when a reader tries the head fetch. But privacy doesn't actually close that: `publish` today publishes an already-existing head CID and has no opinion on whether the block is up, which is exactly what liveness and revival legitimately need. A rotation adapter that went through the port could still upload nothing and publish. So the visibility change buys a guard against one specific bypass shape, with exactly two plausible future callers — rotation's two adapters, both of which this design is writing and reviewing.

The witness already covers the path that matters: an envelope can't reach the network un-preflighted. Someone hand-rolling a `PublishRequest` to dodge that is a code-review question, not a type-system one.

Recommendation: take plain A, skip the privacy change.

content.text: One wrinkle worth surfacing before I write this up: `open_at_floor` — the mechanism #817 named for the dry run — takes signed `record_bytes` and assembles its envelope by *fetching the head block* (`net/child.rs:132-146`). Neither is available pre-publish: `publish` signs internally (`publish.rs:160-162`) and the head block isn't uploaded yet. input.content:
## Resolution

**A custody-free `publish_record` sitting one thin layer above `net::publish::publish`, gated by a preflight witness type, reporting a third `Unconfirmed` outcome.** The port moves bytes to the network and hands back the signed record; it holds no read-key material, seals nothing, and runs no gate.

```
author (caller)      ReadBody -> seal_read_body -> Envelope (+ GrantSection at a scope root)
preflight (caller)   envelope-level unseal + binding check -> PreflightedHead   <- the only constructor
publish_record       upload head block -> net::publish::publish -> signed record bytes
self-adopt (caller)  Candidate from the bytes in hand -> adopt_deferred -> commit floors
```

### The port is custody-free

The decisive fact is `HeldRecord` (`net/liveness.rs:44-52`): it stores the **narrow per-name Ed25519 signer**, explicitly not the scope write seed, because the seed would derive the full write plane for every node in the scope — "least privilege; security rules 2 and 5". A custody-bearing port needs a read key on every publish, so it would either force read keys into the held set against that documented decision, or exclude liveness and revival — at which point it is not the one shared port the map scoped.

This also extends the stance the layer below already takes: `PublishRequest.signer` is "derived in the key-lifecycle slice; injected here so this slice owns no key derivation" (`net/publish.rs:41-43`). The whole net plane is custody-free apart from an injected signer, and stays that way.

The arguments for a custody-bearing port did not survive inspection:

- **"The AAD binding is asserted where the gate re-derives it."** #817 already mandates a dry run before the record reaches the network, and a wrong `(v, id, scope, epoch)` fails that dry run wherever it lives. The dry run is the structural protection, not custody.
- **"Rotation gets its deferred envelope wiring free."** Rotation must unseal the read body to re-seal it at the new epoch, and derives the new read key from the override seed it just minted (`rotation/reseal.rs:198`, which produces a signed `GrantSection` and stops). The port would be handed a key rotation already computed to make a call rotation can make itself — roughly `seal_read_body` → `encode_envelope` → `compute_cid`.
- **"One home for the rule-8 encode guards."** They are already elsewhere and staying: `body.validate()` fires inside `seal_read_body` (`core/seal/envelope.rs:131`), `assert_children_unique` is in core, and the empty-head-CID guard is already in `publish` (`publish.rs:133-135`).

### The witness recovers the one thing custody bought

A custody-free port cannot enforce that what it publishes was ever preflighted. So `PreflightedHead` is a newtype whose only constructor is the preflight function: an un-dry-run envelope cannot be passed to `publish_record`. Structural guarantee, zero key material in the port.

**The preflight is envelope-level, not `open_at_floor`.** #817 named `open_at_floor` as the dry run, and that mechanism does not fit pre-publish: it takes signed `record_bytes` and assembles its envelope by fetching the head block (`net/child.rs:132-146`), while `publish` signs internally (`publish.rs:160-162`) and the block is not uploaded yet. #817's *intent* — a bad encoding fails the op instead of reaching the network — is preserved by the parts of that pipeline that need neither the network nor a record: unseal the read body under the key the gate will re-derive, and check the `id`/`scope`/`epoch` bindings. The full six-stage gate still runs, post-publish, on the returned bytes.

**Consequent requirement on the adopters.** The post-publish self-adopt must not re-fetch a head block the caller is holding. `RootAdopter` and `ChildAdopter` both keep a private `assembled: RefCell<Option<_>>` (`net/adopter.rs:64`, `net/child.rs:52`) that already exists to avoid exactly this re-fetch — the self-adopt path needs a supported way to prime it (or an equivalent locally-supplied-head constructor). Without it, #817's "no fetch" is not achievable.

### `Unconfirmed` — the third outcome

`fanout_get_verify` collapses three situations into `None` (`net/fanout.rs:96-116`): every endpoint erroring, every endpoint serving no record, and every endpoint serving unverifiable garbage. It cannot distinguish "the network is unreadable" from "our record is not there", so today a publish that acked but never became resolvable reports `Published` (`publish.rs:183-190`) — the exact mechanism behind #817's accepted residual.

The port reports `Unconfirmed { sequence, record_bytes }` instead of destroying the distinction, and #819's failure classification decides what it means. Treating it as a `PublishError` was rejected: unresolvability is an availability fact, and this codebase keeps availability and trust strictly apart.

Retrying is cheap because the floor only advances on a gate-passing unseal and the port never adopts: a republish after an `Unconfirmed` reads the same floor and mints the same sequence — a re-PUT of an equivalent record, not sequence churn.

Three rulings follow directly, decided here rather than deferred:

1. **Self-adopt runs only on `Published`.** Adopting an `Unconfirmed` publish would advance the sequence floor and destroy the idempotent-in-sequence retry. On `Unconfirmed` the op stays queued, the snapshot is not seeded, and the write stays visible through the pending-op overlay — which is what the overlay is for (#830).
2. **An `Unconfirmed` op that exhausts #819's attempt budget dead-letters *without* the abandonment retire.** The record may well be live; retiring its CIDs would unpin content a published record points at. This is a carve-out from #819's abandonment rule, on the same logic as #818's: retire only where absence is established, never where it is merely unobserved.
3. **Rotation's adapters map `Unconfirmed` to their existing not-published error** (`ScopeRootPublishError::NotPublished`, `rotation/rotate.rs:70-77`). A rotation must not advance its floor on a cut it cannot confirm.

### Form: a thin module above `publish`, not a replacement

The port cannot replace `net::publish::publish`. Liveness's sub-EOL renewal (`net/liveness.rs:201`) and revival (`net/revival.rs:84`) publish an already-known head CID, author nothing, and have no envelope to preflight — revival recovers its CID from the recovery endpoint. They keep calling `publish` directly. Extending `PublishRequest` with an optional head block and witness was rejected: those fields are `None` for two of its three callers, and the witness would need an "already-adopted bytes" constructor, which is the bypass again with extra steps.

Making `publish` `pub(super)` to close that bypass was costed and rejected as disproportionate. `pub(crate)` would achieve nothing (rotation and the sync drain are in-crate), so it would have to be `pub(super)`; that is free in production — the only non-test callers are already inside `net/` — but breaks nine call sites in `crates/engine/tests/net.rs` (368, 411, 447, 509, 553, 616, 661, 853, 1028), splitting the 1160-line net-plane simulation harness across two homes. The guard also does not close what it appears to: `publish` publishes an existing head CID and has no opinion on whether its block was uploaded, which is precisely what liveness and revival need. A hand-rolled `PublishRequest` is a code-review question, not a type-system one.

A Rust trait was rejected: the net plane is uniformly free functions over seam generics, and rotation's existing traits exist to keep its *orchestration* pure — a second trait behind them adds an indirection with one implementation.

### The interface

```rust
/// A head block that passed the pre-publish preflight (#817). Only `preflight`
/// constructs one, so an un-dry-run envelope cannot reach the network.
pub struct PreflightedHead { /* head_block: Vec<u8>, head_cid: String */ }

/// Envelope-level dry run: unseal under the key the gate will re-derive and
/// check the id/scope/epoch bindings. No network, no record, no floor advance.
pub fn preflight(
    reader: &ReaderContext<'_>,
    envelope: &Envelope,
    section: Option<&GrantSection>,
) -> Result<PreflightedHead, GateError>;

pub struct RecordPublishRequest<'a> {
    pub name: &'a IpnsName,
    pub signer: &'a Ed25519Signer,
    pub head: &'a PreflightedHead,
    pub content_cids: Vec<String>,
    pub min_current_sequence: Option<u64>,
}

pub enum RecordPublishOutcome {
    Published   { sequence: u64, record_bytes: Vec<u8> },
    Unconfirmed { sequence: u64, record_bytes: Vec<u8> },
    LostRace    { published_sequence: u64, observed_sequence: u64 },
}

pub async fn publish_record<T, H, C, F, Sch>(/* seams */, request: &RecordPublishRequest<'_>)
    -> Result<RecordPublishOutcome, RecordPublishError>;
```

Forced consequences, recorded rather than asked:

- **`name` and `signer` are injected, never derived.** Deriving the name needs the write scope seed (`rotation/rotate_write.rs:379-382`, `session.rs:147-152`) — the exact material the held set was narrowed to exclude.
- **The unit is one record per call.** IPNS has no batch PUT; only registration can batch, and `publish` already registers a single-item batch by design ("name waves and sweeps batch — that is the caller's concern", `publish.rs:61-63`). Multi-record ops loop in #819's referent-before-reference order.
- **Sequencing is unchanged.** `floor + 1`, with first publish falling out at 1 from the absent-floor 0 sentinel, and `min_current_sequence` reserved for revival. The port reads the floor and never raises it (#817). Minting `observed + 1` was never on the table: it would supersede a record we have not adopted.
- **Content-block upload stays with the drain.** The port takes CIDs. Rotation republishes existing content and uploads nothing; pulling the staging store into the port would couple it to a plane rotation does not have.

### Call sites that collapse into it

- **The write-plane drain** — its only publish path.
- **`ScopeRootPublisher::publish_scope_root`** (`rotation/rotate.rs:98-107`) and **`WriteWavePublisher::republish`** (`rotation/rotate_write.rs:167`) — their production impls become adapters over `publish_record`, which is the "backing" the map's scoping call described. The traits stay: rotation's tests fake at that boundary extensively, and `is_republished` and `retire` are not publish operations at all.
- **Liveness and revival do not collapse.** They keep calling `publish` directly, for the reasons above.

## Consequences for other tickets

- **#823 (encode-side fail-closed guards)** is unblocked and inherits the witness: `PreflightedHead` is an encode-side guard in the rule-8 sense — a release-active constructor that refuses to produce bytes the decode path would reject. Whether it counts as a fifth guard or subsumes one of the four is that ticket's call.
- **#786 stays a separate slice, but its acceptance criterion needs amending** — see the note posted there.
- **#797 stays a separate slice.** It fixes `HeldMaterial` in the resolve-tick loop, and liveness's renewal never goes through this port at all.
- **#830 (overlay)** gains a case: an `Unconfirmed` op stays in the overlay rather than being seeded into the snapshot.

## Newly surfaced

- **`open_at_floor` cannot serve as #817's pre-publish dry run** — it requires signed record bytes and fetches the head block (`net/child.rs:132-146`). Resolved above by making the preflight envelope-level; recorded because #817's resolution names the mechanism explicitly.
- **The adopters need a supported locally-held-head path** so the post-publish self-adopt does not re-fetch a block the caller holds. The private `assembled` cache in both adopters is the existing shape; it needs an entry point. This is a build-slice requirement for #825, not a fresh decision.

The decisive fact is `HeldRecord` (`net/liveness.rs:44-52`): it stores the **narrow per-name Ed25519 signer**, explicitly not the scope write seed, because the seed would derive the full write plane for every node in the scope — "least privilege; security rules 2 and 5". A custody-bearing port needs a read key on every publish, so it would either force read keys into the held set against that documented decision, or exclude liveness and revival — at which point it is not the one shared port the map scoped.

This also extends the stance the layer below already takes: `PublishRequest.signer` is "derived in the key-lifecycle slice; injected here so this slice owns no key derivation" (`net/publish.rs:41-43`). The whole net plane is custody-free apart from an injected signer, and stays that way.

The arguments for a custody-bearing port did not survive inspection:

- **"The AAD binding is asserted where the gate re-derives it."** #817 already mandates a dry run before the record reaches the network, and a wrong `(v, id, scope, epoch)` fails that dry run wherever it lives. The dry run is the structural protection, not custody.
- **"Rotation gets its deferred envelope wiring free."** Rotation must unseal the read body to re-seal it at the new epoch, and derives the new read key from the override seed it just minted (`rotation/reseal.rs:198`, which produces a signed `GrantSection` and stops). The port would be handed a key rotation already computed to make a call rotation can make itself — roughly `seal_read_body` → `encode_envelope` → `compute_cid`.
- **"One home for the rule-8 encode guards."** They are already elsewhere and staying: `body.validate()` fires inside `seal_read_body` (`core/seal/envelope.rs:131`), `assert_children_unique` is in core, and the empty-head-CID guard is already in `publish` (`publish.rs:133-135`).

### The witness recovers the one thing custody bought

A custody-free port cannot enforce that what it publishes was ever preflighted. So `PreflightedHead` is a newtype whose only constructor is the preflight function: an un-dry-run envelope cannot be passed to `publish_record`. Structural guarantee, zero key material in the port.

**The preflight is envelope-level, not `open_at_floor`.** #817 named `open_at_floor` as the dry run, and that mechanism does not fit pre-publish: it takes signed `record_bytes` and assembles its envelope by fetching the head block (`net/child.rs:132-146`), while `publish` signs internally (`publish.rs:160-162`) and the block is not uploaded yet. #817's *intent* — a bad encoding fails the op instead of reaching the network — is preserved by the parts of that pipeline that need neither the network nor a record: unseal the read body under the key the gate will re-derive, and check the `id`/`scope`/`epoch` bindings. The full six-stage gate still runs, post-publish, on the returned bytes.

**Consequent requirement on the adopters.** The post-publish self-adopt must not re-fetch a head block the caller is holding. `RootAdopter` and `ChildAdopter` both keep a private `assembled: RefCell<Option<_>>` (`net/adopter.rs:64`, `net/child.rs:52`) that already exists to avoid exactly this re-fetch — the self-adopt path needs a supported way to prime it (or an equivalent locally-supplied-head constructor). Without it, #817's "no fetch" is not achievable.

### `Unconfirmed` — the third outcome

`fanout_get_verify` collapses three situations into `None` (`net/fanout.rs:96-116`): every endpoint erroring, every endpoint serving no record, and every endpoint serving unverifiable garbage. It cannot distinguish "the network is unreadable" from "our record is not there", so today a publish that acked but never became resolvable reports `Published` (`publish.rs:183-190`) — the exact mechanism behind #817's accepted residual.

The port reports `Unconfirmed { sequence, record_bytes }` instead of destroying the distinction, and #819's failure classification decides what it means. Treating it as a `PublishError` was rejected: unresolvability is an availability fact, and this codebase keeps availability and trust strictly apart.

Retrying is cheap because the floor only advances on a gate-passing unseal and the port never adopts: a republish after an `Unconfirmed` reads the same floor and mints the same sequence — a re-PUT of an equivalent record, not sequence churn.

Three rulings follow directly, decided here rather than deferred:

1. **Self-adopt runs only on `Published`.** Adopting an `Unconfirmed` publish would advance the sequence floor and destroy the idempotent-in-sequence retry. On `Unconfirmed` the op stays queued, the snapshot is not seeded, and the write stays visible through the pending-op overlay — which is what the overlay is for (#830).
2. **An `Unconfirmed` op that exhausts #819's attempt budget dead-letters *without* the abandonment retire.** The record may well be live; retiring its CIDs would unpin content a published record points at. This is a carve-out from #819's abandonment rule, on the same logic as #818's: retire only where absence is established, never where it is merely unobserved.
3. **Rotation's adapters map `Unconfirmed` to their existing not-published error** (`ScopeRootPublishError::NotPublished`, `rotation/rotate.rs:70-77`). A rotation must not advance its floor on a cut it cannot confirm.

### Form: a thin module above `publish`, not a replacement

The port cannot replace `net::publish::publish`. Liveness's sub-EOL renewal (`net/liveness.rs:201`) and revival (`net/revival.rs:84`) publish an already-known head CID, author nothing, and have no envelope to preflight — revival recovers its CID from the recovery endpoint. They keep calling `publish` directly. Extending `PublishRequest` with an optional head block and witness was rejected: those fields are `None` for two of its three callers, and the witness would need an "already-adopted bytes" constructor, which is the bypass again with extra steps.

Making `publish` `pub(super)` to close that bypass was costed and rejected as disproportionate. `pub(crate)` would achieve nothing (rotation and the sync drain are in-crate), so it would have to be `pub(super)`; that is free in production — the only non-test callers are already inside `net/` — but breaks nine call sites in `crates/engine/tests/net.rs` (368, 411, 447, 509, 553, 616, 661, 853, 1028), splitting the 1160-line net-plane simulation harness across two homes. The guard also does not close what it appears to: `publish` publishes an existing head CID and has no opinion on whether its block was uploaded, which is precisely what liveness and revival need. A hand-rolled `PublishRequest` is a code-review question, not a type-system one.

A Rust trait was rejected: the net plane is uniformly free functions over seam generics, and rotation's existing traits exist to keep its *orchestration* pure — a second trait behind them adds an indirection with one implementation.

### The interface

```rust
/// A head block that passed the pre-publish preflight (#817). Only `preflight`
/// constructs one, so an un-dry-run envelope cannot reach the network.
pub struct PreflightedHead { /* head_block: Vec<u8>, head_cid: String */ }

/// Envelope-level dry run: unseal under the key the gate will re-derive and
/// check the id/scope/epoch bindings. No network, no record, no floor advance.
pub fn preflight(
    reader: &ReaderContext<'_>,
    envelope: &Envelope,
    section: Option<&GrantSection>,
) -> Result<PreflightedHead, GateError>;

pub struct RecordPublishRequest<'a> {
    pub name: &'a IpnsName,
    pub signer: &'a Ed25519Signer,
    pub head: &'a PreflightedHead,
    pub content_cids: Vec<String>,
    pub min_current_sequence: Option<u64>,
}

pub enum RecordPublishOutcome {
    Published   { sequence: u64, record_bytes: Vec<u8> },
    Unconfirmed { sequence: u64, record_bytes: Vec<u8> },
    LostRace    { published_sequence: u64, observed_sequence: u64 },
}

pub async fn publish_record<T, H, C, F, Sch>(/* seams */, request: &RecordPublishRequest<'_>)
    -> Result<RecordPublishOutcome, RecordPublishError>;
```

Forced consequences, recorded rather than asked:

- **`name` and `signer` are injected, never derived.** Deriving the name needs the write scope seed (`rotation/rotate_write.rs:379-382`, `session.rs:147-152`) — the exact material the held set was narrowed to exclude.
- **The unit is one record per call.** IPNS has no batch PUT; only registration can batch, and `publish` already registers a single-item batch by design ("name waves and sweeps batch — that is the caller's concern", `publish.rs:61-63`). Multi-record ops loop in #819's referent-before-reference order.
- **Sequencing is unchanged.** `floor + 1`, with first publish falling out at 1 from the absent-floor 0 sentinel, and `min_current_sequence` reserved for revival. The port reads the floor and never raises it (#817). Minting `observed + 1` was never on the table: it would supersede a record we have not adopted.
- **Content-block upload stays with the drain.** The port takes CIDs. Rotation republishes existing content and uploads nothing; pulling the staging store into the port would couple it to a plane rotation does not have.

### Call sites that collapse into it

- **The write-plane drain** — its only publish path.
- **`ScopeRootPublisher::publish_scope_root`** (`rotation/rotate.rs:98-107`) and **`WriteWavePublisher::republish`** (`rotation/rotate_write.rs:167`) — their production impls become adapters over `publish_record`, which is the "backing" the map's scoping call described. The traits stay: rotation's tests fake at that boundary extensively, and `is_republished` and `retire` are not publish operations at all.
- **Liveness and revival do not collapse.** They keep calling `publish` directly, for the reasons above.

## Consequences for other tickets

- **#823 (encode-side fail-closed guards)** is unblocked and inherits the witness: `PreflightedHead` is an encode-side guard in the rule-8 sense — a release-active constructor that refuses to produce bytes the decode path would reject. Whether it counts as a fifth guard or subsumes one of the four is that ticket's call.
- **#786 stays a separate slice, but its acceptance criterion needs amending** — see the note posted there.
- **#797 stays a separate slice.** It fixes `HeldMaterial` in the resolve-tick loop, and liveness's renewal never goes through this port at all.
- **#830 (overlay)** gains a case: an `Unconfirmed` op stays in the overlay rather than being seeded into the snapshot.

## Newly surfaced

- **`open_at_floor` cannot serve as #817's pre-publish dry run** — it requires signed record bytes and fetches the head block (`net/child.rs:132-146`). Resolved above by making the preflight envelope-level; recorded because #817's resolution names the mechanism explicitly.
- **The adopters need a supported locally-held-head path** so the post-publish self-adopt does not re-fetch a block the caller holds. The private `assembled` cache in both adopters is the existing shape; it needs an entry point. This is a build-slice requirement for #825, not a fresh decision.

input.content:
Three durability/correctness defects in `packages/client/src/seams/stagingStore.ts`, the OPFS half of the `StagingStore` seam. Surfaced by the #829 staging-budget research on map #813; all three are live today and get worse as the write plane lands on top of this seam.

## 1. `putStagedBytes` discards the short-write result (`stagingStore.ts:91`)

```ts
handle.truncate(0);
handle.write(staged, { at: 0 });   // <- return value dropped
handle.flush();
```

`FileSystemSyncAccessHandle.write()` returns the number of bytes actually written. On a quota-exhausted or otherwise constrained write it can return **fewer bytes than requested without throwing**. Today that truncated block is staged silently, `stagedBytesTotal()` under-counts it, and the drain later uploads a short block whose CID does not match the CID the engine computed for the full bytes.

This is the AGENTS.md rule 8 shape at the staging boundary: the read path hard-rejects a body whose bytes do not match its CID (`crates/engine/src/content/read.rs:224-226`), so the produce side must fail closed rather than stage bytes its own reader will always reject. Note the #821 publish-port design does not help here — its preflight is envelope-level and never sees content blocks.

**Fix:** compare the returned count against `staged.byteLength` and throw on a short write. Delete the partial file before throwing so a retry does not resume from a truncated file.

## 2. `stagedBytes` discards the short-read result (`stagingStore.ts:114`)

```ts
const size = handle.getSize();
const out = new Uint8Array(size);
handle.read(out, { at: 0 });        // <- return value dropped
return out;
```

Same shape on the read side: `read()` returns the bytes actually read, and a short read leaves the tail of `out` as zeroes. The caller cannot distinguish that from legitimately-staged data.

**Fix:** compare the returned count against `size` and throw on a short read.

## 3. `navigator.storage.persist()` is never called anywhere

There is no `persist()` call in `packages/client/src` or `apps/web/src`. Without persistent-storage permission, Safari's ITP evicts unvisited origins' storage after seven days — which deletes **the entire durable op queue and every staged byte**, not just cache. That directly contradicts the offline-parity premise the staging design rests on (`crates/engine/src/sync/staging.rs:4-9`): a user who queues work offline and returns must find their queue intact.

**Fix:** request persistence at engine/worker init, before the first enqueue. `persist()` returning `false` is not fatal — durability is best-effort on some browsers — but the result should be surfaced so the host can warn rather than silently promise durability it does not have.

## Acceptance

- Short write and short read each fail closed with a typed error; the partial file is removed on a short write.
- Persistence is requested once at init and the granted/denied result is observable to the host.
- Unit tests in `packages/client` covering both short-count paths with a fake sync access handle. Note the web unit runner only picks up `*.test.ts` — a `.spec.ts` is silently skipped in CI.

Surfaced by #829. Part of #655.

===== 794 =====
core: encode-side recursion depth bound is debug_assert-only, unbounded in release
## Problem

`write_value`'s recursion-depth limit in `crates/core/src/seal/body.rs` is a `debug_assert!(depth < MAX_DEPTH)`, which is **stripped in release builds**. Consequences:

1. **Release build has no recursion bound on the encode path.** A pathologically deep locally-constructed value tree stack-overflows instead of failing closed with an `Err`. This is the exact AGENTS.md rule-8 shape: a debug-only guard on an encode path (encode operates on self-constructed trees, not direct attacker input, so risk is low — but the guard should be release-active).
2. **`seal::body::tests::scrub_runs_when_encode_unwinds` fails under `cargo test --release -p cipherbox-core`** (verified) — the test relies on the `debug_assert!` to trigger the unwind, which does not fire in release, so `encode` does not panic and `result.is_err()` is false. This blocks release-mode `cargo test` for the core crate (CI runs debug, so it is green there).

Confirmed during the #792 (owner-write-blob) crypto-privacy review; pre-existing in untouched `body.rs`.

## Fix

- Promote the encode-side depth check to a **release-active** bound: return `Err` (a `write_value`/`encode` error variant) when `depth >= MAX_DEPTH`, so a deep tree fails closed in release rather than stack-overflowing.
- Fix the test to force a genuine release-active unwind (e.g. gate on `#[cfg(debug_assertions)]` or construct a condition that fires in release) so `cargo test --release -p cipherbox-core` passes.

Part of #752.


===== 827 =====
engine: mailbox client routes miss the API path prefix and have no contract coverage
## Defect

All three of the engine API client's mailbox methods target routes the API does not serve. Every one will 404 on first use.

| Client method | Path sent | Path served |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mailbox_post` (`crates/engine/src/api/client.rs:306`, path at `:327`) | `POST /mailbox` | `POST /mailbox/messages` |
| `mailbox_poll` (`client.rs:336`, path at `:338`) | `GET /mailbox` | `GET /mailbox/messages` |
| `mailbox_ack` (`client.rs:357`, path at `:359`) | `DELETE /mailbox/{id}` | `DELETE /mailbox/messages/{id}` |

The API side is `@Controller('mailbox')` with `@Post('messages')`, `@Get('messages')`, and `@Delete('messages/:id')` (`apps/api/src/mailbox/mailbox.controller.ts:30,34,58,72`). `apps/api/openapi.json` declares only `/mailbox/messages` and `/mailbox/messages/{id}`.

## Why it was not caught

The contract suite has **no mailbox coverage at all** — `grep -rn mailbox crates/contract/tests/` returns nothing. Per AGENTS.md the live contract suite is the enforcement mechanism for the API contract, since there are no generated clients, so this is a gap in the gate rather than a flake.

The mismatch is latent today only because no production code calls these methods yet — the grants/mailbox engine logic that would exercise them has not been wired.

## Fix

1. Correct the three paths in `crates/engine/src/api/client.rs`.
2. Add mailbox coverage to the contract suite so the route set is enforced going forward — post, poll, and ack against a real API instance.

## Provenance

Fo
===== 798 =====
test(engine): extract the shared owner-root head-block fixture to testkit
The owner-root head-block builder (owner blob → write body → owner-write-blob → grant section → `seal_read_body` → envelope → head CID) is duplicated ~130 LOC across `crates/engine/src/net/adopter.rs` (`Fixture::build`, fixed consts `[0x44]`/`[0x55]`, standalone owner keys) and `crates/engine/src/facade.rs` (`owner_root()`, the all-zero bootstrap anchor derived from `CAP_SECRET` so the engine's own session opens it).

**Acceptance:** extract one parameterized builder into `testkit` (e.g. `owner_root_fixture(scope, root, keys)`) taking the diverging inputs (scope/root ids, key source) as parameters, and use it from both sites.

Flagged by the #789 simplify review (Medium — the single biggest tightening opportunity). Part of #752.

**[#827](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/827)** — all three engine mailbox client methods target routes the API doesn't serve (`/mailbox` vs `/mailbox/messages`, `api/client.rs:327,338,359`). Guaranteed 404 on first use, latent only because nothing calls them yet. The fix is three strings; the real work is adding mailbox coverage to the contract suite, which has none at all — and per AGENTS.md that suite *is* the API contract enforcement, so this is a gate hole, not a flake.

**[#798](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/798)** — ~130 LOC of duplicated owner-root head-block fixture across `net/adopter.rs` and `facade.rs`. Pure test refactor, and it happens to sit exactly where #821's "adopters need a locally-supplied head path" requirement will land, so doing it first makes that slice cleaner.

**What I'd leave alone right now:**

- [#812](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/812) (encode-side guards for child read-path rejects) looks like a twin of #794, but map ticket [#823](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/823) — which I just unblocked — is precisely the decision about *which layer owns those guards*. Starting #812 now risks implementing the answer before it's made.
- [#705](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/705) is already folded into map ticket [#822](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/822) by an explicit scoping call.
- [#786](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/786), [#797](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/797), [#752](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/752) are all write-plane and under active design.
- [#703](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/703) (revival corroborating its recovered sequence against the durable floor) is now *better informed* than when it was filed — #821 confirmed `min_current_sequence` stays revival's alone — but it's a fail-closed judgment call, not mechanical.

Want me to launch #794 and #827 now? They're in disjoint crates and each gets its own worktree, so they won't collide with each other or with #833. I'd hold #798 until one of the others lands, since a testkit refactor touching `net/adopter.rs` could conflict with whatever #823 turns into.

Part of #813

## Question

AGENTS.md rule 8 requires every decode-side hard reject to have a matching **release-active** `Err` on the produce path — never `debug_assert!`. #812 lists four such debts, each explicitly waiting on the write plane:

1. **Grant section on a child envelope** — child adoption rejects any envelope carrying a `grantSection` key (`has_grant_section`, `crates/core/src/seal/envelope.rs`); child envelope sealing must refuse to attach one.

Read all four. Two of them aren't forks at all, one has a false fork in the ticket, and one is a real choice.

**Guards 2 and 4 are free structurally in the engine — no check needed.** Guard 2 (kind transplant) is inherently cross-record: `ChildRef.kind` lives in the *parent's* read body, the sealed body kind in the *child's*. Core can never see both, so no core-side option exists. But if the authoring function takes one `NodeKind` and uses it for both the child's `ReadBody` variant and the parent's `ChildRef.kind`, disagreement is unrepresentable. Same for guard 4: the engine already derives names as a typed `IpnsName` (`rotation/rotate_write.rs:379-382`), so authoring that writes `name.as_str().as_bytes()` into `ChildRef.ipns_name` cannot emit a non-canonical form. Making `ChildRef.ipns_name` a typed field in core was the alternative and it's actively worse — it would move the rejection into `decode_read_body`, so one malformed child ref would make an entire folder unreadable instead of failing just that child.

**Guard 3's fork as written is not available.** The ticket says enforcing in core means changing `Version::new` to take something `SealedContent`-derived. Core can't: `assemble`, `decode_root`, and `RootManifest` all live in `crates/engine/src/content/dag.rs:106,159`, and core cannot depend on engine. #820's own title — "define its **engine-side** KAT vector" — confirms the DAG codec stays engine-side deliberately. So guard 3 is the engine's either way; only the *form* is open.

Sizing it, since it's cheaper than the ticket implies: `Version::new` has **eight call sites and zero production callers** (`seal_props.rs:79`, `kat_gen.rs:2495/2496/2678`, `body.rs:578/579/716`, `facade.rs:3285`), and the wire bytes are untouched because `to_value`/`from_value` don't change — so no KAT vector regenerates differently. `SealedContent` (`content/mod.rs:48-56`) has no `size` field, but `seal_content` already computes `plaintext.len()` and hands it to `assemble`, so adding one is about two lines.

- **Structural:** `SealedContent` gains `size`; one engine constructor builds the `Version` from it, so `contentCid` and `size` come from the same value and cannot disagree. Costs ~2 lines plus a constructor. Against: core's `Version::new` stays public and reachable, so the guarantee holds along the authoring path only — it's unrepresentable-by-construction where we build records, not globally.
- **Checked:** a release-active `Err` at the authoring call site comparing the two. Against: per-callsite, exactly the failure mode #812 exists to fix, and it needs a release-build test to prove the check fires.

**Guard 1 is the real choice.** `seal_read_body` returns `unknown: Vec::new()`; the grant section is attached by the caller pushing `("grantSection", …)` onto the public `Envelope.unknown`. Core already owns the decode-side predicate `has_grant_section` (`envelope.rs:91`).

- **Core-side `encode_child_envelope`:** rejects when `has_grant_section`, sitting directly beside its decode twin. ~10 lines, no call-site churn, and the symmetry is self-documenting. *Against:* it's a second encode entry point — `encode_envelope` still exists and a child authored through it bypasses the guard entirely.
- **Engine-side, structural:** the engine's child-authoring path is the only producer of child envelopes and simply never attaches a section. *Against:* nothing stops a future caller from pushing onto `unknown` directly; the guard is a convention, not a type.
- **Make `Envelope.unknown` private with a typed attach:** genuinely structural. *Against:* `unknown` exists to preserve forward-compatible fields across decode→encode, so privatising it means designing a preservation API — real work in a frozen codec, well beyond this ticket.

Worth separating, because core-side is only actually on the table for one of them.

**Guard 3 has no core-side option.** `assemble`, `decode_root`, and `RootManifest` live in `crates/engine/src/content/dag.rs` and core cannot depend on engine. So three of the four are engine-side regardless — the choice is real only for guard 1.

**What engine-side buys on guard 1:**

- **Core cannot actually check what the guard claims.** `Envelope` is one type; "child" vs "scope root" is a fact about the tree that only the engine knows. A core `encode_child_envelope` checks for a *marker*, dressed up as a check on a *role* — hand it a root envelope and it rejects wrongly; hand a child to plain `encode_envelope` and it doesn't fire. The name promises more than the function can deliver.
- **The bypass can't be closed from core anyway.** `encode_envelope` has to stay public for roots, so the core-side guard is opt-in — the same per-callsite weakness, but paid for with new surface in the frozen crate.
- **Rule 8's produce path is the authoring layer, not the codec.** `encode_envelope` serialises what it's handed; it isn't the thing that decides a record's shape. Putting the guard there conflates "encode these bytes" with "author this record".
- **All four guards end up in one place.** Since 2, 3, and 4 must be engine-side, putting 1 there too gives one authoring layer, one review surface, one test suite — rather than three guards in engine and one lone guard in core, reviewed and tested differently.
- **Budget.** Core is KAT-frozen and every change there pulls a crypto review. Engine-side costs nothing from that budget.

**What you'd give up:** adjacency. The reason rule-8 violations keep recurring here is that the two halves drift apart, and a guard sitting literally beside `has_grant_section` is hard to drift from. Core-side also protects every future consumer, not just this engine.

There's a third shape that gets both: **the engine's child-authoring calls core's `has_grant_section` release-active.** Core keeps the single shared predicate it already has, the engine owns the produce-path decision, and the two halves cannot drift because they're the same function. No new core surface, no role semantics in core, and all four guards stay in one layer.

All four workers are now briefed on the full `/ship` loop. Here's what changed and what I'll do while you're out.

**What my original briefs were missing:** `/verify` (drive the flow end-to-end, not just tests), the full local PR-gate suites rather than just the touched package, the CodeRabbit CLI pass, the three-way triage rule with **discard as the default**, and the resolve-reviews loop. Also three environment facts a fresh subagent can't know: `git push`/`git fetch` are sandbox-blocked, `gh pr edit` fails on this repo so bodies must be patched via `gh api`, and bare `#NN` needs escaping in PR bodies.

I tailored the `/verify` step per worker, since it means something different in each case — for [#827](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/827) it's the contract suite against a live stack (ship.md calls that the only live client→API gate, and that ticket exists *because* the gate was empty); for [#794](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/794) it's `cargo test --release -p cipherbox-core` actually passing; for [#798](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/798) it's proving neither call site's assertions got weaker in the move, which is the real failure mode for a test refactor that stays green by testing less.

**The one thing I'm handling centrally rather than delegating:** CodeRabbit's web review auto-fires on `gh pr ready` and is capped at one per hour org-wide. Four PRs marked ready together means three get no web review at all. So each worker stops after pushing its draft PR and running the CLI pass, and I'll mark them ready one at a time, wait for each review to land, then hand that PR to a dedicated resolve-reviews agent. That's roughly a four-hour sequence — fine while you're AFK, but it does mean the last PR won't be green until well after the first.

I've also recorded that `/ship` exists as the canonical brief, so I stop hand-rolling a subset of it.

Two things I'll leave for your call rather than deciding alone: **merges** — ship.md explicitly leaves the merge decision to the user, so all four will end green-and-ready but unmerged. And if a worker hits a gate it genuinely can't fix — most plausibly #827 failing to get a live API up — I'll leave the PR draft with the gap stated plainly rather than marking it ready on unverified work.

The map is at a clean stopping point: [the publish port](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/821) and [the encode-side guards](https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/issues/823) are both closed and recorded, and the six-ticket frontier is all HITL, so nothing there moves without you.

| Method | Was | Now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mailbox_post` | `POST /mailbox` | `POST /mailbox/messages` |

## Problem

`THROTTLE_SURFACES.auth` is `{ limit: 10, ttl: 60_000 }` (`apps/api/src/ops/throttling.ts:11`) and is applied per-IP to the login-shaped endpoints — `POST /auth/challenge` and `POST /auth/login` among them (`apps/api/src/auth/auth.controller.ts:59,71,92,102,117,171`).

The contract suite currently sits at **exactly 10/10** on that bucket. It passes, but with no margin: **one additional identity login anywhere in `crates/contract/tests/contract.rs` will 429 and fail the whole suite**, and the failure will present as an unrelated auth error rather than as a rate limit, so the next person to hit it will lose time diagnosing it.

This is why the mailbox tests added in #835 mint accounts via `test_login` (its own bucket, 3/10) rather than `fresh_account`. That is a workaround, not a fix — `test_login`'"'"'s bucket has 7 slots left and the same cliff behind it.

## Why it matters now

The contract suite is the only live client→API integration gate (AGENTS.md; `blueprint/testing.md`), so it is the suite most likely to keep growing. A gate that silently caps how many tests can be added is a gate that will start being worked around instead of extended.

## Options to weigh

- Raise the `auth` limit under the test profile only, keeping production limits intact.
- Share one authenticated session across tests that do not need a distinct identity.
- Reset the throttler store between tests (the storage backend would need to be reachable from the harness).
- Key the throttle by something other than IP when running against a test profile.

## Acceptance

The contract suite can add a new account-minting test without approaching the bucket, and a throttle-induced failure surfaces as an explicit rate-limit diagnostic rather than a generic auth failure.

<result>PR #834 is up to date and CI is green so far. Final report:

## Branch & PR
- Branch: `fix/opfs-staging-short-io` (head `5229a52c0`, 4 commits)
- PR: https://github.com/FSM1/cipher-box/pull/834 — **draft**, `Closes #833`. Not marked ready, as instructed.
- Final diff: 6 files, +326/−9, all under `packages/client/src`.

## The three defects
1. **Short write (`stagingStore.ts:91`)** — `handle.write()` returns a byte count and a quota-constrained write reports a short count without throwing. The count is now compared against the copied payload length; a mismatch deletes the partial file (after the handle is closed, so a retry starts from empty rather than resuming a truncated file) and throws a typed `StagingIoError`. If the cleanup itself fails, the short-write error still wins and carries the cleanup failure as its `cause`.
2. **Short read (`stagingStore.ts:114`)** — same shape; a short read left the tail of the output buffer zeroed and indistinguishable from staged data. Now compared against `getSize()` and rejected. The `NotFoundError`-tolerant delete was extracted into one `removeIfPresent` helper shared with `removeStagedBytes`.
3. **`navigator.storage.persist()`** — now requested once in `EngineClient` construction (UI realm), before any tab can enqueue, and reported to the host via a new `onStoragePersistence` config callback. Denial is reported, never thrown.

## Verification (step 1) — this caught a real bug
I first implemented defect 3 in the engine **worker** bootstrap, as the issue words it. **Verification run:** `cargo test --release -p cipherbox-core` (all pass), `cargo test --release -p cipherbox-engine` (all pass).

**Issues:** 0 critical, 0 high, 1 medium (already fixed in the working tree — see below), 1 low, 2 nits.

### IMPORTANT PROCESS NOTE FIRST

`/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/.claude/worktrees/agent-a8f13a19beada004a/crates/engine/src/rotation/reseal.rs` has **uncommitted working-tree changes** that are not in `origin/main...HEAD`. ### [MEDIUM — present in committed HEAD, fixed uncommitted] HPKE ephemeral scalar left un-zeroized on the new error paths

**Location:** `/Users/myankelev/Code/random/cipher-box/.claude/worktrees/agent-a8f13a19beada004a/crates/engine/src/rotation/reseal.rs` — four sites, at HEAD lines ~259, ~283, ~309, ~333.

Committed shape:

```rust
let mut ephemeral = fill::<32, E>(entropy)?;          // plain [u8; 32], not Zeroizing
let sealed = seal_grant_blob(&recipient_pub, &ephemeral, &ctx, &payload)
    .map_err(ResealError::Encode)?;                    // <-- early return jumps the wipe
ephemeral.zeroize();
```

**Issue:** `fill::<32, E>` (reseal.rs:178-182) returns a bare `[u8; N]` with no `Drop` wipe. The new `?` returns past `ephemeral.zeroize()`, stranding a live HPKE X25519 ephemeral scalar on the stack. Rule 7 (terminal-owner) violation: `ephemeral` is owned here, so this frame is the terminal owner and must wipe on every exit.

**Impact:** Bounded. The error is structurally unreachable (see the reachability analysis under item 4), so no reachable path leaks. Even if reached, encode fails *before* `hpke_seal` is called, so the scalar was never used to derive a shared secret — recovering it yields nothing. This is discipline, not an exploitable leak.

**Recommendation:** exactly what the working tree already does — bind the `Result`, wipe, then `?`:

```rust
let sealed = seal_grant_blob(&recipient_pub, &ephemeral, &ctx, &payload);
ephemeral.zeroize();
let sealed = sealed.map_err(ResealError::Encode)?;
```

Applied at all four sites (grant blob, owner blob, owner-write blob, ascent link). Verified correct: the `&ephemeral` borrow ends before the wipe, and `payload` (whose `SecretBytes` fields own the seeds) drops-and-zeroizes on the error return regardless. The `seal_history_link` site (reseal.rs:355) needs nothing — `nonce` is public and `HistoryLinkPayload` self-zeroizes on drop. **Stronger long-term fix:** make `fill` return `Zeroizing<[u8; N]>` so this class cannot recur; the manual-wipe pattern is one `?` away from breaking every time this function is edited.

---

### [LOW] `pub fn encode_fixed_depth` is a panicking public API on a WASM target

**Location:** `crates/core/src/codec/encode.rs:45-47`

**Issue:** `encode(value).expect(...)` is `pub`. It must be `pub` (the engine calls it from `content/dag.rs:124` and `grants/accept.rs:65`), so exposure is justified. But `crates/core` compiles to WASM under `panic=abort`, where a panic aborts the whole instance rather than unwinding — a single future misuse turns a malformed remote record into a client-wide DoS instead of a `CodecError`.

**Reachability: unreachable at every current call site.** I enumerated all nine:

| Call site | Tree shape | Max node depth |
|---|---|---|
| `seal/aad.rs:137` `build_aad` | array of scalars | 1 |
| `seal/structure.rs:83` `structure_sig_preimage` | flat map of scalars | 1 |
| `payload/mailbox.rs:65` `sig_preimage` | array of scalars | 1 |
| `payload/mailbox.rs:95,104` `seal_mailbox_payload` | flat maps | 1 |
| `payload/pointer.rs:109,116` `seal_pointer_payload` | `{object:{…scalars}, ownerSig}` | 2 |
| `ipns/record.rs:236` `encode_data` | flat map of scalars | 1 |
| `suite/contact.rs:38,113` | flat maps of scalars | 1 |
| `engine/content/dag.rs:124` `assemble` | map + array of `Bytes` CIDs | 2 |
| `engine/grants/accept.rs:65` `SharePointer::encode` | flat map | 1 |

None accepts a caller/attacker-supplied `Value` subtree. Verified `crates/wasm/src` does not re-export it to the JS surface.

**Forward hazard worth flagging (not a defect in this PR):** `RepointObject::from_value` (`crates/core/src/payload/pointer.rs:395`-ish) currently **drops** unknown fields rather than preserving them. If someone later brings it in line with `blueprint/core.md` D10 ("tolerate + round-trip, one policy") by adding an `unknown: Vec<(String, Value)>` passthrough, `seal_pointer_payload`'s `encode_fixed_depth` instantly becomes attacker-reachable and the panic becomes a live remote DoS. That is the single highest-risk call site.

**Recommendation:** keep the API, but pin the assumption mechanically rather than by doc comment — a unit test asserting `encoded_depth(tree) <= 2` for each fixed-shape builder, or (cheaper) a one-line note on `RepointObject` that adding unknown-field preservation requires switching `seal_pointer_payload` to fallible `encode`. Not a merge blocker.

### [NIT] `encode_map_partial` can drop a partially-written, unreserved buffer on the new `?`

**Location:** `crates/core/src/codec/fields.rs:105`

`out` is `Vec::new()` and grows by reallocation, and the new `write_value(&mut out, value, 1)?` can now return mid-write, dropping it un-zeroized. Both the single-reservation invariant (encode.rs:21-29 doctrine) and scrub-on-error are absent here. **Not a live issue:** grep confirms zero production callers — only `crates/core/tests/codec_props.rs`, `tests/kat_manifest.rs`, and `examples/kat_gen.rs`. Worth a one-line doc note that this path is not secret-safe, so a future production caller does not silently inherit both gaps.

The `WriteBodyEncode` → `Encode` rename (reseal.rs:138-141, 157, 172) has no consumer anywhere (grep across `crates/`, `packages/`, `apps/` finds only the definition), and no test asserts either the old or new `"structure-encode-failed"` string. Correctly classified as non-retryable in `crates/engine/src/rotation/cascade.rs:311` (`is_retryable` matches only `Entropy`), so the fail-closed semantics are right — but the variant is entirely untested. ## Judgments on the five questions asked

**1. Zeroization discipline — one real gap, already fixed uncommitted.** Every new `?` in `crates/core` is on the *result of* `encode(...)`, i.e. before any secret buffer exists in the caller's frame, so there is nothing to wipe on those returns. The transient secret-bearing `Value` trees are guarded correctly: `ScrubOnDrop` is constructed *before* the `encode(guard.0)` tail expression at `seal/body.rs:392` (`encode_read_body`) and `seal/grant.rs:227` / `:360` / `:501` / `:739` (grant blob, override seed, owner-write blob, history link), so `Drop` runs on `Err` identically to `Ok`. `pointer.rs:171` (`encode(object_value)?` in `decode_and_verify`) creates no buffer on the error path. The only gap was reseal.rs, above.

Notably, `crates/core/src/seal/body.rs:743` — the old `scrub_runs_when_encode_unwinds` test — is now `scrub_runs_when_encode_fails_closed` and no longer needs `catch_unwind` or the `#[cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))]` gate. That is a genuine improvement: the guard's error-path behavior is now covered on the WASM leg too, which the `panic=abort` carve-out previously excluded.

**2. Encode/decode fail-closed symmetry — exact, no off-by-one.** Encoder: `check_depth(depth, …)` rejects on `depth >= MAX_DEPTH` (encode.rs:87-91), entered at `depth = 0` from `encode` (encode.rs:33) and `encoded_len` (encode.rs:56), incremented once per array item and once per map value. Decoder: identical predicate at `decode.rs:151`, entered at `read_value(0)` from `decode.rs:16`, incremented at `decode.rs:169` / `decode.rs:177`. Map *keys* increment neither side. Both therefore admit exactly max-node-depth ≤ 127 and reject 128. Confirmed empirically, not just by inspection: the KAT accept vector `array-nested-at-depth-limit-128` (`crates/core/kat/vectors/codec/accept.json:251`, 128 nested array heads with the innermost at depth 127) is decoded and re-encoded byte-identically by `accept_vectors_decode_reencode_and_render_diag` (`crates/core/tests/kat_manifest.rs:1445`) — which passes under `--release`. That test would fail on a tightening off-by-one; the new `encode_rejects_past_max_depth` (encode.rs:250-259) would fail on a loosening one. Both directions are pinned.

**3. Determinism and wire stability — no byte changes.** `count_value` reproduces the old `encoded_len` term-for-term: `head_len(n)` for uints, `head_len(len)+len` for bytes, `text_len` for text, `head_len(count)` plus recursion for arrays, `head_len(count) + Σ(text_len(k) + …)` for maps, `1` for bool/null. Only the accumulation style changed (`+=` into `&mut usize` vs `.sum()`); overflow semantics are identical and the >2^64-byte precondition is unreachable. The single-reservation security invariant is not merely preserved but *strengthened*: because `encoded_len` runs first inside `encode` (encode.rs:32) and is now bounded, `Vec::with_capacity` is never reached on a failing tree — so `out` is never allocated, let alone partially filled with secrets and freed. A corollary worth stating: `write_value(…)?` inside `encode` is now an unreachable `Err`, since `count_value` and `write_value` traverse the identical tree in the identical depth-first order and must fail at the same node. That is fine as defense-in-depth. No encoder output path changed; `encode_fixed_depth` is `encode` on success, so AAD, all signature preimages, and IPNS `data` bytes are bit-identical.

**4. `encode_fixed_depth`'s `expect` — unreachable everywhere today.** Full call-site table above; `pub` is required by two engine call sites and is acceptable. See the LOW finding for the one forward hazard.

**5. No weakening of the adoption gate, preimages, AAD, or KDF catalog.** `build_aad`'s array positions, `structure_sig_preimage`'s map, the mailbox sig preimage (including the `#712` recipient binding), and the whole KDF edge catalog are untouched — only the encode call is renamed. Engine changes to `adopter.rs` and `facade.rs` are test-fixture `?`/`.unwrap()` churn only. `ResealError::Encode` is classified non-retryable at `cascade.rs:311`, so a depth or duplicate-tag encode failure aborts the rotation cascade fail-closed rather than being retried as an availability stall. Rule 8 is satisfied at the level it demands: the check is release-active and covered by tests that fire in a release build (confirmed by running the suite with `--release`).

**One pre-existing rule-8 residue, noted not charged:** `encode_read_body` (`crates/core/src/seal/body.rs:349`) still guards child uniqueness with `debug_assert!` only. It is defensible because the persist boundary `seal_read_body` (`envelope.rs:131`) calls `body.validate()?` release-active first, and the PR's own doc edit says so. But since this PR exists precisely to retire the last encode-side `debug_assert`, leaving one behind in the same function invites the next reviewer to re-litigate it. Either promote it to a release-active `Err` (the `assert_children_unique` convention AGENTS.md cites) or leave it — but expect CodeRabbit/Greptile to flag it.

---

## Suggested tests (beyond what the PR adds)

```rust
// crates/core/src/codec/encode.rs — pins symmetry, not just the reject side.
#[test]
fn deepest_admissible_tree_round_trips() {
    let v = nested(crate::codec::MAX_DEPTH - 1);
    let bytes = encode(&v).expect("deepest admissible tree encodes");
    assert_eq!(crate::codec::decode(&bytes).unwrap(), v, "encoder and decoder admit the same domain");
    assert_eq!(encoded_len(&v).unwrap(), bytes.len());
}

// A tolerantly-decoded unknown-field subtree at max depth must re-encode,
// i.e. no codec re-nests a decoded subtree deeper than it was read.
#[test]
fn max_depth_unknown_field_survives_decode_reencode() { /* build a read-body whose
   unknown field carries nested(MAX_DEPTH - 2); decode_read_body then
   encode_read_body must be Ok and byte-stable */ }

// crates/engine/src/rotation/reseal.rs — the untested error variant.
#[test]
fn reseal_fails_closed_on_write_body_encode() {
    // duplicate ledger tag -> ResealError::Encode, check() == "structure-encode-failed",
    // and CascadeError::is_retryable() == false.
}
```

## Recommendations, in order

1. **Commit the working-tree `reseal.rs` fix.** Reviewing `origin/main...HEAD` alone sees the un-zeroized ephemeral. Consider folding in `fill -> Zeroizing<[u8; N]>` so the manual-wipe pattern cannot regress on the next edit.
2. Add the `deepest_admissible_tree_round_trips` test — the PR pins the reject side and the KAT pins the accept side, but nothing in `encode.rs` itself asserts both halves of the boundary together.
3. Leave `encode_fixed_depth` `pub`; add the `RepointObject` forward-hazard note or the depth-≤2 guard test.

No blocking crypto or privacy defect. The core design decision — making the *first* pass (`encoded_len`) bounded so the failing path never allocates a secret-bearing buffer — is the right one and is what keeps this change zeroization-neutral.</result>
